#10222. New in llama.cpp: Model Management

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

This feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:

This auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

You can also point to a local directory of GGUF files:

On the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:

All loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:

The built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.

Have questions or feedback? Drop a comment below or open an issue on GitHub.

Supported via presets.ini, where you can specify the mmproj (and other long and short arguments) per model.

#10220. This celebrity’s unhinged Letterboxd reviews take comedy to a new level

Letterboxd is known for its quippy film reviews, and the platform’s newest member fits right in: Philomena Cunk.

For the uninitiated, Cunk is a world-renowned journalist, acclaimed for her work on the documentaries Cunk on Britain, Cunk on Earth, and Cunk on Life. Cunk may not know much about the subjects she covers, and she may put her interview subjects in uncomfortable positions—but on the bright side, she also isn’t real.

Cunk is a character portrayed by English comedian Diane Morgan. For her next mockumentary series, Morgan as Cunk is tackling the history of filmmaking in Cunk on Cinema.

How better to let her fellow cinephiles know about the new series, than to meet them where they’re at? Hence her new Letterboxd account, @cunkoncinema, with which Cunk joins the 30 million movie lovers already on the app.

“Done a show about cinema so the producers made me set this up for PR reasons,” reads the account’s bio. “They’re literally watching me type this now.”

So far, Cunk has left 18 reviews in her signature deadpan, which translates even over text. Her first review was for E.T.: “Basically a kid finds a little old man hiding from the police in his shed. The old man gets the kid drunk and says nobody must know about their friendship. A lot of fingering. In the end, the old man gets locked and is taken away in a prison ship. I cried.” Cunk gave the film five stars.

Other five-star entries on Cunk’s Letterboxd include The Wizard of Oz, which she called a “garish film about colours for drag queens and under fives,” and Die Hard, which she said is “not just Christmassy, which makes you think.”

Meanwhile, she’s panned movies including Rain Man and The Wicker Man, both dubbed “disappointing superhero films,” and Thor: The Dark World. “Dark. Couldn’t see anything,” Cunk wrote.

Cunk is leaving more reviews every day, presumably leading up to the series’ release. On November 10, she continued her streak of movies with “Seven” in their titles: Following Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs and Seven Samurai, she watched Seven Brides for Seven Brothers, which she assumed was a “spin off from Seven, with Brad Pitt and also spin off from the Bride of Frankenstein, not with Brad Pitt.”

Giving the internet a taste of Cunk’s movie taste might be the perfect primer for Cunk on Cinema, which will feature out-there interviews with Hollywood icons like composer Daniel Pemberton, director Michael Bay, and actor Benedict Cumberbatch.

Cunk on Cinema comes to Netflix on November 15.

#10218. 7 E-commerce UX Tips for Selling Car Accessories and Home & Kitchen Products Online

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Here is a question a product page should answer in about five seconds: “Will this magnetic phone mount hold my phone with the case still on?” When the answer is hard to find, shoppers tend to open another tab instead of contacting support.

Stores that sell both car accessories and home & kitchen products face an extra challenge: two very different catalogs share one site. A car accessories buyer cares about fit, mounting and compatibility. A home & kitchen buyer cares about size, capacity and how easy the product is to clean. A single generic product page frustrates both.

This guide covers seven practical e-commerce UX tips that designers and developers can apply right away, with code snippets and a checklist at the end.

A car mount and a vegetable peeler should not share the same spec table. Keep a single reusable product page component and change only the fields based on category. The layout stays consistent, while each shopper sees the details they need.

In code, this can be a config object that your template reads from:

Showing “Not specified” instead of hiding a missing field is a small habit with a real benefit: it makes gaps in your product data visible to your own team.

Shoppers look for deal-breaker information near the price and the purchase button: fit, size and compatibility. Do not bury it in an “Additional information” tab halfway down the page.

A short comparison table also works better than three paragraphs of marketing copy, because shoppers scan rather than read. Baymard Institute’s product page research consistently finds that unclear or hard-to-find specifications are a common reason shoppers hesitate.

A responsive layout is the starting point, not the finish line. People compare car accessories in a parking lot and browse kitchen gadgets while standing in the kitchen, often with one thumb.

A phone mount on a white background says nothing about how it attaches to a dashboard. Show it in a real car, from the driver’s point of view. For home & kitchen products, place the item next to something familiar, like a coffee mug, so people can judge its size.

Good alt text matters for accessibility and for image search. Compare “phone mount” with “Magnetic phone mount fixed to a car dashboard, holding a phone in landscape mode”. The W3C alt text decision tree is a useful guide for deciding what to describe.

Keep images fast, too. Responsive sources with srcset and sizes, explicit dimensions and lazy loading help prevent layout shift and slow pages:

One caveat: do not lazy-load the main product image at the top of the page. It is usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, so web.dev advises loading it eagerly.

Shoppers often search for a problem rather than a product. Few people type “seat gap filler” the first time; they type “stuff falling between car seats”. Your search, synonyms and category names should handle both.

Mixed catalogs show why this matters. Stores that cover both vehicle and household products, such as VNSPORT.org with its separate product collections, keep the two audiences apart so that someone looking for a dashboard mount never has to scroll past kitchen tools. The principle applies to any store with more than one audience: group by the shopper’s intent, not by your supplier list.

Decorative “100% secure” badges do little. What builds trust is information shoppers can check for themselves:

At checkout, show the full cost, including shipping and taxes, before payment, let people fix mistakes easily and offer guest checkout. In Baymard’s checkout usability research, unexpected extra costs and forced account creation are among the top reasons shoppers abandon a cart.

If your support inbox gets the same question every week, the product page has a gap. Answer it on the page, close to where the decision happens, instead of on a generic help page three clicks away.

You can mark up those answers with FAQPage structured data:

A reality check: since 2023, Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health websites. Do not add FAQs just to chase a snippet. Add them because they answer real questions and help shoppers decide.

What are the most important e-commerce UX tips for a car accessories store? Show compatibility and mounting details next to the price, use in-car photos, and make sure the mobile layout works with one hand.

How should product pages differ for car accessories and home & kitchen products? Use the same layout but different spec fields. Car accessories need fit, mounting and power details. Home & kitchen products need dimensions, capacity, materials and cleaning instructions.

How big should buttons be on a mobile product page? WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum target size of 24 × 24 CSS pixels. For primary actions such as “Add to cart”, around 44 pixels is more comfortable.

Do FAQ sections still help SEO? Mostly indirectly. FAQ rich results are now limited, but clear on-page answers can match long-tail searches, reduce returns and keep shoppers on the page.

How can I reduce cart abandonment? Show total costs early, offer guest checkout, display delivery times and return terms before payment, and keep the checkout form short.

Good e-commerce UX is not about clever animations. It is about answering the shopper’s question before they have to ask it. Clear specs, honest photos, thumb-friendly controls and real FAQs turn an ordinary product page into one that helps people buy, whether they are shopping for car accessories or home & kitchen essentials.

#10217. CUGA on Hugging Face: Democratizing Configurable AI Agents

AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge. Many existing frameworks struggle with brittleness, tool misuse, and failures when faced with complex workflows.

CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations. It's an open-source, AI Agent that combines flexibility, reliability, and ease of use for enterprise use cases. By abstracting orchestration complexity, CUGA empowers developers to focus on domain requirements rather than the internals of agent building. And now, with its integration into 🚀Hugging Face Spaces🚀, experimenting with CUGA and open models has never been easier.

CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments. It has achieved state-of-the-art performance on leading benchmarks:

🥇 #1 on AppWorld - a benchmark with 750 real-world tasks across 457 APIs

🥈 Top-tier on WebArena (#1 from 02/25 - 09/25) - showcases CUGA Computer Use capabilities with a complex benchmark for autonomous web agents across application domains

We're also continuing to innovate with new experimental capabilities, including:

The CUGA architecture begins with the user's message flowing into a chat layer that interprets intent and constructs the user's goal, based on context. A task planning and control component then decomposes this goal into structured subtasks, tracked programmatically through a dynamic task ledger. This ledger supports re-planning when needed, ensuring robust execution. Subtasks are delegated to specialized agents, such as the API agent, which uses an inner reasoning loop to generate pseudo-code instructions before invoking code in a secure sandbox. The system leverages a tool registry that goes beyond MCP protocols to parse and understand tool capabilities, enabling precise orchestration. Once all steps are completed, the final response is returned to the user, delivering reliable, policy-aligned outcomes.

CUGA works best when inference is fast. When each call takes seconds, delays compound and force a tradeoff between agent capability and user experience. Running on high-performance inference platforms like Groq shows how fast inference fundamentally expands what agent architectures can achieve.

CUGA is fully open source, under the Apache 2.0 license, and you can find us at cuga.dev.

By embracing open models, CUGA aligns with the Hugging Face ethos of democratizing AI-giving developers the freedom to choose models that best fit their needs, whether for experimentation or production.

CUGA has been tested with a variety of open models, including gpt-oss-120b and Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-fp8 (both hosted on Groq). Our Hugging Face Space uses gpt-oss-120b, with the model hosted on Groq, offering a rapid response time for LLM calls

Groq runs open models on its custom‑built LPUs, which are designed for AI inference and optimal for repeated agent inferences required by CUGA's architecture, enabling planning, execution, and validation steps to finish fast. The result is strong cost and performance: open models are ~80-90% cheaper than closed alternatives; Groq's OpenAI-compatible APIs meet production latency needs, and CUGA stays fully configurable across models, providers, and deployment topologies.

To make agent development even more accessible, CUGA integrates with Langflow, an open-source visual programming interface for building LLM-powered workflows. Its intuitive drag-and-drop interface reduces the barrier to entry for those who prefer low-code solutions.

Starting with Langflow 1.7.0, CUGA ships with its own widget, enabling users to assemble complex, multi-tool agents visually and deploy with a click. Give it a try at langflow.org.

We've launched a CUGA demo on Hugging Face Spaces to give you a taste of what's possible. This demo showcases a small CRM system and equips CUGA with 20 preconfigured tools for handling sales related data queries and API interactions through the API Agent. To make experimentation even more powerful, the demo provides access to workspace files, enabling you to use predefined policies.

Give it a try on Hugging Face Spaces and share your feedback!

CUGA brings a new level of flexibility and openness to AI agent building. To engage with us:

Configurable Generalist Agent, leader in AppWorld Benchmark

Impressive work on CUGA’s architecture and configurability. The structured planning, tool orchestration, and benchmark results demonstrate a strong approach to scalable agent design. Integration with Hugging Face Spaces and Langflow significantly lowers the barrier to experimentation and deployment.Here is our Website: https://www.simbainstitute.in/artificial-intelligence-course-in-surat/

Rent abroad or buy compliant cards: both of China’s routes to Nvidia compute are running short.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia-based compute is getting scarce and expensive for Chinese AI labs on both of their main routes, buying export-compliant cards and renting abroad, and the Financial Times reports that Nvidia’s own crackdowns are part of the reason. Nvidia has told cloud partners worldwide that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese firms, while Chinese companies have bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation cards this year to cover the shortfall. Meanwhile, a B300 rack that sells for about $600,000 internationally reportedly fetched $2.8 million in China last month.

Chinese customers have ordered more than 6 million of Nvidia’s export-compliant RTX Pro 5500 cards. That is at least twice the 3 million that the company could reportedly manufacture in 2027. One source told CNBC that it was proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront, in comparison to a non-Chinese entity.

Many Chinese groups have relied on overseas leases for advanced AI work, which can include model training, and these tech groups have been the biggest clients for data centers in Southeast Asia. Data centers unable to find non-Chinese clients could be forced to pull back supply, and it’s “difficult to find enough non-Chinese clients outside the US,” one Singapore-based group told the FT. While Nvidia hasn’t confirmed or denied its new rule, implementing it would ease criticism from U.S. lawmakers just as Chinese demand is growing.

What Nvidia told partners has come through verbal instructions, via sales and regional teams, and applies globally rather than just in Asia. Existing deals and leases are not changed, but new ones must comply. Nvidia’s whitelist more than halved its authorized Asian buyer count, which encouraged more Chinese groups to lease over other options, including smuggling. On top of this, Fleet Intelligence tracking is now required for Southeast Asian providers that want to become Nvidia Cloud Partners. All of these combined — whitelist, cap, and tracking — may act to alleviate U.S. concerns.

Among companies that have moved to renting, Moonshot has held discussions to rent capacity from neoclouds that host in Europe with Nvidia GPUs. Specifically, it’s looking for Nvidia Blackwell systems, which export controls bar from China; one source said the talks covered clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs in Europe. These clusters would handle inference, serving models to end users, and the European talks for them happened after the White House said Moonshot accessed Blackwell chips through a facility in Thailand. The firm has been fervent about its intentions to secure more compute.

Moonshot isn't the only Chinese company looking to secure Nvidia chips for AI training. Tencent has a deal with Oracle to lease 100,000 GPUs in Southeast Asian data centers. ByteDance and Alibaba are also pursuing similar long-term leases, and most of these overseas data centers run chips like the forbidden B300. MiniMax, like Moonshot, also leases significant compute both at home and abroad.

The big reason is that domestic AI chip supply is simply not up to the task, although not for a lack of trying. Huawei is expected to hit 1.6 million chips this year, with about 1 million from Alibaba and Baidu, and 300,000 from Cambricon. Total supply this year will be up to 3.5 million, including about 1 million made overseas, against a demand that far exceeds 5 million. That number could more than double next year.

Part of the problem is that the export-compliant cards Chinese firms have been buying, mostly the RTX Pro 6000D, RTX Pro 5000, and RTX 5090, are mostly useful for simpler work such as prefill. Even so, the discontinued 6000D’s pricing in China has reportedly doubled. Huawei’s Ascend 910C outperforms them in most areas, but these lower-end options are still coveted, partly because of a preference for CUDA over Huawei’s CANN. Nvidia’s programming platform is supported by most AI frameworks and libraries, and much in-house code is optimized for it.

Then there’s the RTX Pro 5500, with 84GB of GDDR7 with ECC and 1,398 GB/s of memory bandwidth. The card runs on a full PCIe Gen 5 x16 interface, draws up to 600 W, and can be split into up to two MIG instances. That still leaves it well short of a B300, which has about 3.4 times the memory and 5.7 times the bandwidth, plus NVLink, which the 5500 lacks.

Export-compliant; samples in December, deliveries from Q1 2027

Licensed by the U.S. case by case; Beijing withholding approval for large-scale imports

Indicated orders from China are not precise, but the total of over six million includes more than three million from ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent. The big three ordered at about $11,400 each, for a total sticker price over $35 billion. This is difficult to fill when there may be fewer than three million produced next year, and partners might only actually get 5% to 10% of the original ask. Starting in 2027, much of Nvidia’s TSMC capacity may shift to Rubin, taking more production, while the RTX Pro 5500’s early samples are due in December.

On the legal side, it’s currently easier to rent than to own as current U.S. law does not give regulators broad authority over overseas cloud access. The Remote Access Security Act (RASA), which would extend U.S. export controls to that area, has sailed through the House but has not yet passed the Senate. Those directly affected — neoclouds and related financiers — price in a possible ban regardless, which drives the upfront premium.

China’s side is not completely clean, either, with about 600,000 H200s reportedly stuck in storage in Hong Kong awaiting shipment to the mainland. Beijing is withholding approvals for large-volume imports such as this. Only relatively small quantities have come in during recent months, for some big internet companies, with others coming through intermediaries and indirect routes in small quantities. The price: over $900,000 for an eight-card H200 server in China at the end of last month, about 3x the cost a year ago. This is despite the fact that H200 sales are already under U.S. license.

The first test that will show how many cards will actually land occurs in Q1 2027, when the RTX Pro 5500 is expected in commercial deliveries. For rentals, whether or not the Remote Access Security Act is a factor depends on a Senate vote, which is not yet scheduled. Nvidia’s Q3 results come in soon, on Nov. 17, which could bring some illumination.

With CEO Jensen Huang under scrutiny lately over reports that he was targeted by an alleged Chinese spy, which Nvidia’s board is now investigating, he’s going to feel the heat even more just a day later, when lawmakers have asked him to attend a closed-door briefing. He’s been pushing for laxer controls and more access, so the assumed 51% rule will also be put to the test.

#10215. Taking Ozempic or Wegovy? The FDA says there’s a new warning you shouldn’t ignore

The FDA is adding a new warning label onto GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Zepbound for a rare side effect with serious risk. 

All GLP-1 drug makers will now be required to include new safety warnings informing patients that the medications could increase risk of sudden vision loss from a condition known as nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). The condition, which is not common, can lead to sudden decreased vision in one eye and even permanent vision loss. The condition’s causes aren’t fully understood, but it happens when blood flow to the front of the optic nerve decreases. 

“NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 [receptor agonist] products,” the FDA wrote in its new guidance. The new warning will appear on all GLP-1 drugs, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, Mounjaro, older GLP-1 agonists, and Foundayo, Eli Lilly’s new GLP-1 pill. The information will appear in the “warnings and precautions” section of prescription labels for the popular drugs. 

Ozempic and other GLP-1 drugs have been hailed as a modern medical miracle, treating everything from diabetes and obesity to kidney disease to addiction. But even as the drugs become much more widely prescribed, researchers continue to learn about what they can do and how they work. That could mean more warning labels in the future. 

Correlation not causation

The FDA began exploring the connection between GLP-1 drugs and vision loss after a 2024 study found that use of semaglutide in diabetes patients was associated with NAION. The study’s observational design means it can’t prove a causal link between semaglutide-based GLP-1 drugs and vision loss from the condition, but the research was enough to prompt the agency to launch “comprehensive evaluation” of research on the topic, including clinical trial data, animal data, case reports, and other observational studies. 

A causal link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION is also complicated by the fact that underlying conditions that the drugs are designed to treat can also increase risk of the rare vision loss condition. “Risk factors may include smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia, and kidney disease,” the FDA’s report noted. GLP-1s are prescribed for both diabetes and weight management. 

Last year, the European Medicines Agency issued its own findings on the topic. “Results from several large epidemiological studies suggest that exposure to semaglutide in adults with type 2 diabetes is associated with an approximately two-fold increase in the risk of developing NAION compared with people not taking the medicine,” the agency wrote. It recommended that semaglutide drugs include a side effect warning for NAION categorized as “very rare” and noted that the condition could affect 1 in 10,000 people using the drugs.

The FDA similarly found the risk of vision loss very low, but statistically significant enough to report. “Based on published literature, the incidence of NAION in the general population is 2.3 to 10.2 cases per 100,000 persons per year in adults older than age 50,” according to the FDA. Anyone who experiences sudden, painless changes to vision in one eye should immediately report their symptoms to their health provider.

#10213. Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy is powering a new class of realistic meme that Nvidia made possible

The scandal surrounding Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with an alleged spy has escaped the sandbox of Silicon Valley and spread across social media.

But in one particularly bizarre corner of the internet, a cinematic universe inspired by the affair is spawning AI-generated music videos and short films starring the Nvidia CEO.

Nvidia’s stock has taken a hit since the reveal, losing nearly $700 billion in market value amid ongoing scrutiny. The semiconductor giant has opened an investigation into Huang and the spying allegations.

A cinematic universe powered by AI

Meanwhile, creators on social media are taking a different approach to the situation, making Huang, his wife, and Alice Huang the stars of hyper-realistic AI-generated videos inspired by pop culture—all without their consent.

In one video posted to X, Huang sings Shaggy’s Wasn’t Me. He wasn’t alone: Other tech leaders like Jeff Bezos, Richard Branson, and Elon Musk join Huang in the AI music video, belting the famous lines “wasn’t me.”

In another, Huang is joined by Alice Huang, reenacting the viral ROSÉ and Bruno Mars APT music video, set against a pink background with exaggerated singing.

The two can also be spotted on an AI recreation of Drake’s Hotline Bling music video and George Michael’s Careless Whisper.

Others inserted Huang into popular movie scenes, like one video reimagining the viral “why would I deceive you” exchange between Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.

Another sets Huang and the businesswoman in the elevator scene made famous by Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Zooey Deschanel in the romcom (500) Days of Summer, or the viral club scene from Three Steps Above Heaven.

Brought to you by … Nvidia’s own tech

The irony of the trend is hard to escape. Generating such detailed videos of real people is only possible thanks to the technology that Huang has helped create and scale—Nvidia’s powerful GPUs.

“Whether someone uses a cloud tool or runs a model on their own machine, the heavy lifting is usually completed by Nvidia GPUs, simply because that’s the hardware that most AI software is built to run on,” Ricardo Amper, CEO of AI identity verification company Incode Technologies, tells Fast Company.

And oten, these videos are made using the Nvidia technology, even inadvertently.

“Most people making AI videos never touch a GPU. They open a browser, type a prompt or upload a photo,” says Michael Bismuth, cofounder of AI-production studio Cuz.

For some creators, the sudden demand for Huang Spy Scandal content has even become a platform to advertise their own AI products, like one cofounder who created a microdrama inspired by the affair.

Sophia Xing, founder of AI microdrama production platform PlotParty, posted a microdrama made with the software, with the quintessential clichéd script, a revenge arch, and an overly long and descriptive title: I Divorced My Trillionaire Husband and the God of Compute Let Me Respawn at 19.

None of it would be possible with out the company at the heart of the scandal. “Nvidia’s chips are the engine behind almost every fake video on the internet,” Bismuth says. “The company that made AI video possible is now one of its targets.”

#10211. The Open Evaluation Standard: Benchmarking NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano with NeMo Evaluator

It has become increasingly challenging to assess whether a model’s reported improvements reflect genuine advances or variations in evaluation conditions, dataset composition, or training data that mirrors benchmark tasks. The NVIDIA Nemotron approach to openness addresses this by publishing transparent and reproducible evaluation recipes that make results independently verifiable.

NVIDIA released Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with an explicitly open evaluation approach to make that distinction clear. Alongside the model card, we are publishing the complete evaluation recipe used to generate the results, built with the NVIDIA NeMo Evaluator library, so anyone can rerun the evaluation pipeline, inspect the artifacts, and analyze the outcomes independently.

We believe that open innovation is the foundation of AI progress. This level of transparency matters because most model evaluations omit critical details. Configs, prompts, harness versions, runtime settings, and logs are often missing or underspecified, and even small differences in these parameters can materially change results. Without a complete recipe, it’s nearly impossible to tell whether a model is genuinely more intelligent or simply optimized for a benchmark.

This blog shows developers exactly how to reproduce the evaluation behind Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B using fully open tools, configurations, and artifacts. You’ll learn how the evaluation was run, why the methodology matters, and how to execute the same end-to-end workflow using the NeMo Evaluator library so you can verify results, compare models consistently, and build transparent evaluation pipelines of your own.

Developers and researchers need evaluation workflows they can rely on, not one-off scripts that behave differently from model to model. NeMo Evaluator provides a unified way to define benchmarks, prompts, configuration, and runtime behavior once, then reuse that methodology across models and releases. This avoids the common scenario where the evaluation setup quietly changes between runs, making comparisons over time difficult or misleading.

Model outputs can vary by inference backend and configuration, so evaluation tools should never be tied to a single inference solution. Locking an evaluation tool to one inference solution would limit its usefulness. NeMo Evaluator avoids this by separating the evaluation pipeline from the inference backend, allowing the same configuration to run against hosted endpoints, local deployments, or third-party providers. This separation enables meaningful comparisons even when you change infrastructure or inference engines.

Many evaluation pipelines work once and then break down as the scope expands. NeMo Evaluator is designed to scale from quick, single-benchmark validation to full model card suites and repeated evaluations across multiple models. The launcher, artifact layout, and configuration model support ongoing workflows, not just isolated experiments, so teams can maintain consistent evaluation practices over time.

Transparent evaluation requires more than final scores. Each evaluation run produces structured results and logs by default, making it easy to inspect how scores were computed, understand score calculations, debug unexpected behavior, and conduct deeper analysis. Each component of the evaluation is captured and reproducible.

By releasing Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with its full evaluation recipe, NVIDIA is providing a reference methodology that the community can run, inspect, and build upon. Using the same configuration and tools brings consistency to how benchmarks are selected, executed, and interpreted, enabling more reliable comparisons across models, providers, and releases.

Open evaluation means publishing not just the final results, but the full methodology behind them, so benchmarks are run consistently, and results can be compared meaningfully over time. For Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B, this includes open‑source tooling, transparent configurations, and reproducible artifacts that anyone can run end‑to‑end.

NeMo Evaluator is an open-source library designed for robust, reproducible, and scalable evaluation of generative models. Instead of introducing yet another standalone benchmark runner, it acts as a unifying orchestration layer that brings multiple evaluation harnesses under a single, consistent interface.

Under this architecture, NeMo Evaluator integrates and coordinates hundreds of benchmarks from many widely used evaluation harnesses, including NeMo Skills for Nemotron instruction-following, tool use, and agentic evaluations, as well as the LM Evaluation Harness for base model and pre-training benchmarks, and many more (full benchmark catalog). Each harness retains its native logic, datasets, and scoring semantics, while NeMo Evaluator standardizes how they are configured, executed, and logged.

This provides two practical advantages: teams can run diverse benchmark categories using a single configuration without rewriting custom evaluation scripts, and results from different harnesses are stored and inspected in a consistent, predictable way, even when the underlying tasks differ. The same orchestration framework used internally by NVIDIA’s Nemotron research and model‑evaluation teams is now available to the community, enabling developers to run heterogeneous, multi‑harness evaluations through a shared, auditable workflow.

Using the same configuration means running the same evaluation methodology.

Each evaluation run produces structured, inspectable outputs, including per‑task results.json files, execution logs for debugging and auditability, and artifacts organized by task for easy comparison. This structure makes it possible to understand not only the final scores, but also how those scores were produced and to perform deeper analysis of model behavior.

The key requirement is access to the model, either as weights you can serve or as an endpoint you can call. For this tutorial, we use the hosted endpoint on build.nvidia.com.

This tutorial reproduces the evaluation results for NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B using NeMo Evaluator. The step-by-step tutorial, including the published configs used for the model card evaluation, is available on GitHub. Although we have focused this tutorial on the Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B, we also published recipes for the base model evaluation.

When reproducing evaluations, you may observe small differences in final scores across runs. This variance reflects the probabilistic nature of LLMs rather than an issue with the evaluation pipeline. Modern evaluation introduces several sources of non‑determinism: decoding settings, repeated trials, judge‑based scoring, parallel execution, and differences in serving infrastructure. All of which can lead to slight fluctuations.

When these elements are consistent, your results represent a valid reproduction of the methodology, even if individual runs differ slightly. NeMo Evaluator simplifies this process, tying benchmark definitions, prompts, runtime settings, and inference configuration into a single auditable workflow to minimize inconsistencies.

The evaluation recipe released alongside Nemotron 3 Nano represents a meaningful step toward a more transparent and reliable approach to open-model evaluation. We are moving away from evaluation as a collection of bespoke, "black box" scripts, and towards a defined system where benchmark selection, prompts, and execution semantics are encoded into a transparent workflow.

For developers and researchers, this transparency changes what it means to share results. A score is only as trustworthy as the methodology behind it and making that methodology public is what enables the community to verify claims, compare models fairly, and continue building on shared foundations. With open evaluation configurations, open artifacts, and open tooling, Nemotron 3 Nano demonstrates what that commitment to openness looks like in practice.

NeMo Evaluator supports this shift by providing a consistent benchmarking methodology across models, releases, and inference environments. The objective isn’t identical numbers on every run; it’s confidence in an evaluation methodology that is explicit, inspectable, and repeatable. And for organizations that need automated or large‑scale evaluation pipelines, a separate microservice offering provides an enterprise‑ready NeMo Evaluator microservice built on the same evaluation principles.

Use the published NeMo Evaluator evaluation configuration for an end-to-end walkthrough of the evaluation recipe.

NeMo Evaluator is fully open source, and community input is essential to shaping the future of open evaluation. If there’s a benchmark you’d like us to support or an improvement you want to propose, open an issue, or contribute directly on GitHub. Your contributions help strengthen the ecosystem and advance a shared, transparent standard for evaluating generative models.

#10210. Gen Z and millennials are rapidly taking advantage of this health insurance tip for freelancers

When Madelyn Roman, 31, wanted to go freelance, the biggest barrier she faced wasn’t how she would make money, but how she would afford healthcare. 

Like many people in the U.S., Madelyn’s health insurance was tied to her employer. But then she learned about a way to get health insurance through her fiancé. (And no, it wasn’t pushing forward the wedding.).

Once a common method for same-sex couples to gain basic rights previously denied to them but long associated with “traditional” marriage, ranging from shared healthcare to inheritance, couples of all sexual orientations are now getting domestic partnerships as a precursor—or alternative—to marriage. 

In the U.S., domestic partnerships can offer benefits such as access to a partner’s employee healthcare, hospital visitation rights, and veteran benefits. 

For New York City-based Roman, and many other freelancers, that right to healthcare can be life-changing, especially since the number of freelancers is rising fast in the U.S. According to FlexJobs, the U.S. has 72 million independent workers, a number that is expected to rise to 86.5 million next year. 

“As a healthcare professional myself, I’ve always taken advantage of my insurance plan,” says Roman. “I need it for both my physical and mental health care services, which I rely on. Life is too unpredictable to go without coverage. Now I have so much freedom to do what I want to do and to work how I want to work.”

Ohio-based Brooke had already made the jump to freelancing while on her parents’ insurance. She was getting closer to aging out of their coverage, but Brooke and her partner weren’t ready to get married. (Some sources in this story withheld their last name for privacy reasons.) 

Yet, with multiple high-risk health conditions, Brooke couldn’t risk any gap in coverage. The couple chose to get a domestic partnership. “We both acknowledged my desperate need for healthcare and are in a committed, loving relationship, so a domestic partnership felt like the best option for us,” says Brooke.

For other couples, the ability to freelance is a bonus to what they see as a way to commit without getting married. Gabrielle, 31, and her partner for a number of years aren’t in a rush to get married. When her coworker mentioned the domestic partnership option, it sounded like the perfect alternative. 

As they were making the decision, Gabrielle, also based in New York City, was offered an exciting freelance role in advertising. “This job opportunity came up and the timing kind of aligned perfectly with taking this next step in our relationship,” says Gabrielle. “I would’ve done it job offer or no job offer, but it felt like a little nod from the universe that I was on the right path.”

A domestic partnership can be a great way to show your commitment without the cost of a wedding. According to The Knot, the average U.S. wedding cost $34,000 in 2025. The average cost per guest rose to $292 from $214 in 2019. Meanwhile, domestic partnerships rarely come in at over $50. 

Domestic partnerships appear especially popular with younger generations. The New York Times reports that the Manhattan City Clerk’s Office registered domestic partnerships for 3,686 millennials and 460 Gen Zers, out of 6,004 in total for 2019. Just five years later, those numbers rose to 4,106 millennials and 1,774 Gen Zers, out of 6,910. 

A 2024 Upwork study found that 53% of Gen Z work as full-time freelancers. 

What are the requirements for a domestic partnership?

So, who can get a domestic partnership? With no nationwide law, state and local officials regulate domestic partnership availability and the rights they afforded.

Typical requirements include both people being 18 years of age or older, currently living together, and not related in any way that would ban a marriage.

It’s usually required that neither person is in a domestic partnership or marriage. Notably, on November 3, domestic partnerships for polyamorous couples were approved in West Hollywood, California, the Los Angeles Times reports. 

A domestic partnership is available in states such as California, Hawaii, Maine, Nevada, New York, Ohio, and Oregon. 

What is the process of obtaining a domestic partnership?

The exact steps for getting a domestic partnership can vary, but typically, applicants

fill out a selection of personal questions online and get an appointment at their local courthouse. Questions might include straightforward things like “Where were you born?” and “Where do you live?” For Americans, whether it’s available where you live, and what the process looks like there, should be available on your state or city’s website. 

As Gabrielle explains, “We filled out an application online, then just brought our identification to the courthouse and they gave us a certificate of domestic partnership. You could literally get one in five minutes.” 

Roman seconds that: “When our number was called, we simply walked up to the window, provided our proof and confirmation number, and paid the small fee. Simple as that. We were then handed an official paper that proves we are domestic partners.”

The domestic partnerships are often done in the same area as courthouse marriages. Roman remembers how some couples showed up in sweatpants, while others were dressed up with a photographer in tow. “Slightly crumpled paper hearts lined the walls, but it was charming,” she says. 

From there, they each registered on their partner’s employee health insurance and got freelancing. 

One catch to keep in mind is whether or not the partner’s employee healthcare allows domestic partners to join it. Finding out if the option is available to non-spouses is a critical step before pursuing a domestic partnership. 

A domestic partnership can also be limiting in that it doesn’t offer the same federal benefits and doesn’t allow the pair to file joint taxes. 

Each of the women emphasize how grateful they are to have this option available to them. 

“It allows me freedom to make income without having to tie it to healthcare,” says Roman. “The job change has been both liberating and great for my mental health. I’m lucky to have such a supportive partner, and to live in a city that provides this option.” 

Brooke echoes that statement, thankful for her partner and this option to access her medication. 

As to whether she would recommend a domestic partnership to other people, Gabrielle puts it simply: “If one partner has a stable, full-time job and the other wants to take a risk, go for it.”

A former employee of The Ethereum Foundation is suing the nonprofit, alleging disability discrimination, retaliation, unfair employment practices, and related claims, reports The Denver Post. 'The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,' a 38-page vision for the next 1,000 years, was distributed to the organization's ~250 employees in Q1 this year. On page 11 of the finalized document, there was a bizarre and rather extreme oath. This illustrated page essentially formed a suicide pledge and, unsurprisingly, scores of people didn't want to sign.

At the top of this story, you can see page 11 from the evidence submitted in the case of FULTON v. ETHEREUM ASIA PACIFIC LIMITED et al. Perhaps one could say it was illustrated like an anime version of Grimm’s fairy tales. Indeed, it contains more than a touch of the macabre, like all the best such stories.

On this particular page, reproduced in court documents, anyone working on the software used by the Ethereum Federation (EF) was asked to ensure that the source code and associated documents remained free and publicly accessible. Underlining this pledge, folks had to vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license, or upon modification or removal of any part of this license.” The message about falling on one’s sword was repeated in the illustration by a cartoon cat.

At the end of the 38-page document, employees picked one of two options, basically agreeing to commit to the direction of the mandate, or not. Choosing the former meant you signed up to this cult-like pact. The latter choice would mean that you were requesting a settlement payment and would “leave the EF without delay.”

This unsettling contractual suicide agreement went out as a draft in late February, and The Denver Post says that resistance to signing such an agreement was “swift and vocal.” About 80 of the Ethereum Federation’s 250-ish employees voted to nix the suicide pledge. Nevertheless, when the mandate was sent around in its final version in March, the suicide pledge remained – albeit in the form of a text with illustration – rather than in the body of the copy.

As the ‘Source Seppuku License’ had basically morphed into an artwork, rather than part of the main text of the mandate, the EF would subsequently argue that the suicide pledge to employees was just “part of the artwork of the mandate.” Importantly, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin insists that the artwork was “not meant to be taken literally.”

In March, resistance to the mandate, led by then-employee Kayleen Fulton, culminated in a response letter endorsing the general direction of the document but declining to tick any boxes, and declining to resign. Though this formal but quiet revolt bore 53 names, only Boulder woman Fulton and a colleague who helped organize the letter were fired.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The reasoning for Fulton being singled out was simple, according to a quote published by the Denver Post, cryptocurrency founder Buterin reportedly said that you should not “reward making a stink with outcomes.” By September, eight senior employees had left the EF, with most of the 53 protest letter signees either resigning or being terminated.

Fulton, who was on a salary of $195,000 per year as a lead in the Protocol Support team, is seeking unspecified damages from the Ethereum Foundation. She also disclosed her ovarian cancer diagnosis to the company on March 24, 2026, roughly two weeks before being fired. The lawsuit thus also claims interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act.

#10208. Top 6 AI YouTube Transcript Generators: Features, Accuracy, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A one-hour YouTube talk contains roughly nine thousand words, and finding the one point you need can take longer than watching the whole thing. A transcript solves that. With text in hand you can search for a phrase, quote an expert accurately, turn a webinar into a blog post, create subtitles or feed a summary tool.

Plenty of tools now promise instant YouTube transcripts, but they work in different ways. Some read the captions YouTube already has. Others listen to the audio themselves and produce a fresh transcript. That difference affects accuracy, speed and cost more than any feature list does. This guide compares six options, explains how each works and points out where each one falls short. Plans and limits change often, so confirm current details on each vendor's site.

Caption extraction. The tool pulls the captions attached to a video, either written by the creator or generated automatically by YouTube. It is fast and usually free, but it is only as good as those captions. YouTube notes that its automatic captions come from machine learning, so quality may vary, and accents, background noise and overlapping speakers can cause errors. Captions may also be missing entirely for some videos.

Fresh speech recognition. The tool takes the audio and runs its own speech-to-text model. This can be more accurate on difficult recordings and works when no captions exist, but it takes longer and often costs money.

Lynote is built for exactly this job. Paste a YouTube link, search by keyword or add a playlist, and it returns a timestamped transcript with an AI summary. Batch mode accepts up to 10 videos at once. The tool lists transcription in more than 100 languages, translation into 25, auto-chapters, one-click copy and TXT download, with SRT export also mentioned. The page says transcripts are free, with no sign-up required.

Best for: Students, researchers and marketers who want a quick, readable transcript or summary from a public video without installing anything.

Limitations: It extracts YouTube captions, so videos without captions cannot be processed. If the original captions are poor, the transcript will be too. For critical accuracy, review the text or use a service with human verification.

Before you install anything, check what YouTube already gives you. Many videos show a transcript option in the description area, and creators can review and edit automatic captions in YouTube Studio under Subtitles. YouTube offers automatic captions in dozens of languages for long-form videos and Shorts.

Best for: Quick lookups on videos that already have decent captions.

Limitations: Captions may not generate for videos with poor sound, long silences, overlapping speakers, mixed languages or unsupported languages. Export options are minimal, and there is no summary or cleanup.

Notta transcribes uploaded audio and video files and also accepts YouTube links. It lists support for 58 languages, real-time and bilingual transcription, and AI Notes that produce summaries and action items. A free plan includes 120 transcription minutes per month at the time of writing.

Best for: Professionals who handle a mix of recordings, meetings and YouTube videos in one place.

Limitations: The free minutes disappear quickly if you process long videos, and the strongest features sit behind paid plans.

Descript is an audio and video editor built around text. It transcribes recordings automatically, and deleting a word in the transcript removes the matching footage. You can import video, audio or a Zoom recording, and there is a free tier that does not require a credit card.

Best for: Creators who want to clean up their own videos and podcasts, not just read a transcript.

Limitations: It is an editor first, so it is more than you need for a quick YouTube lookup. It works with files you own, so you need the source media rather than a public link.

Rev offers both AI and human transcription. It advertises AI transcripts at 96 percent or better accuracy in minutes, and human transcripts at 99 percent or better, guaranteed within 12 hours. AI transcription covers 37 or more languages, while human transcription is English only. Pay-as-you-go rates start at $0.25 per minute for AI, and human transcription is listed at $1.99 per minute.

Best for: Legal, research and media work where mistakes are costly and a human check is worth paying for.

Limitations: The cost climbs for long videos, and the human option is slower than instant AI tools. Those accuracy figures are the vendor's own claims, so test your own audio.

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, released under the MIT license. It handles multilingual transcription, translation into English and language identification. You install it with pip and need ffmpeg, and it comes in several model sizes from tiny to large, so you can trade speed against accuracy and hardware demands.

Best for: Developers building their own pipeline and teams with sensitive audio they prefer to keep on their own machines.

Limitations: You supply the audio, which means downloading it yourself and respecting the video owner's rights and YouTube's terms. Larger models need a capable GPU, and there is no built-in interface for non-technical users.

Start with the source. If the video already has good captions, a link-based tool is the fastest route. If the audio is difficult or the stakes are high, pick a tool that runs its own recognition or offers human review. If you are processing hundreds of videos or handling private recordings, look at Whisper or a paid platform with bulk features.

Whatever you choose, treat the transcript as a first draft. Check names, numbers and technical terms against the video before you publish or quote anything, and credit the original creator.

There is no single best transcript generator. Caption-based tools are quick and free, recognition-based tools are better when captions fall short, and human-verified services make sense when accuracy matters most. Try two or three on a video you know well, compare the results and keep a human in the loop for anything you publish.

Can I get a transcript if a video has no captions? Caption-extraction tools cannot. You need a tool that runs its own speech recognition on the audio, such as the options above that transcribe files.

Are AI transcripts accurate enough to publish? Often they are close, but not perfect. Accents, noise and technical terms cause mistakes, so review before publishing.

Is it legal to transcribe someone else's YouTube video? Transcribing for personal research or accessibility is common, but republishing the text may infringe copyright. Check the video's license and YouTube's terms, and get permission when in doubt.

What is the difference between a transcript and subtitles? A transcript is the full text, while subtitles are timed text shown on screen. Many tools can export both, often as SRT files.

#10206. Tokenization in Transformers v5: Simpler, Clearer, and More Modular

Transformers v5 redesigns how tokenizers work. The big tokenizers reformat separates tokenizer design from trained vocabulary (much like how PyTorch separates neural network architecture from learned weights). The result is tokenizers you can inspect, customize, and train from scratch with far less friction.

TL;DR: This blog explains how tokenization works in Transformers and why v5 is a major redesign, with clearer internals, a clean class hierarchy, and a single fast backend. It’s a practical guide for anyone who wants to understand, customize, or train model-specific tokenizers instead of treating them as black boxes.

For experts: If you're already familiar with the concepts and want to understand the changes in v5, go to v5 Separates Tokenizer Architecture from Trained Vocab

Before diving into the changes, let's quickly cover what tokenization does and how the pieces fit together.

Language models don't read raw text. They consume sequences of integers usually called token IDs or input IDs. Tokenization is the process of converting raw text into these token IDs. (Try the tokenization playground here to visualize tokenization.)

Tokenization is a broad concept used across natural language processing and text processing generally. This post focuses specifically on tokenization for Large Language Models (LLMs) using the transformers and tokenizers libraries.

Ġworld (above) is a single token that represents the character sequence " world" (with the space).

A token is the smallest string unit the model sees. It can be a character, word, or subword chunk like "play" or "##ing" ("##" is a pattern, don't worry if you don't completely understand it now 🤗). The vocabulary maps each unique token to the token ID.

A good tokenizer compresses text into the smallest amount of tokens. Fewer tokens means more usable context without increasing model size. Training a tokenizer boils down to finding the best compression rules for your datasets. For example, if you work on Chinese corpus you can sometimes find very nice surprises 😉.

Tokenization happens in stages. Each stage transforms text before passing it to the next:

Each component is independent. You can swap normalizers or change the algorithm without rewriting everything else.

You can access the rust based tokenizer through _tokenizer. We go in more depth about it in this section

The following algorithms dominate modern language model tokenizers:

The tokenizers library is a Rust-based tokenization engine. It is fast, efficient, and completely language model agnostic. The library handles the mechanics of converting text into token IDs and back. The tokenizers library is a general-purpose tool that implements the tokenization algorithms, but does not implement the conventions that connect those algorithms to specific language models.

Consider what happens when you use tokenizers directly with the SmolLM3-3B model:

The output is raw tokenization. You get token IDs and the string pieces they correspond to. Nothing more.

Now consider what's missing. The SmolLM3-3B is a conversational model. When you interact with it, you typically structure your input as a conversation with roles like "user" and "assistant". The language model expects special formatting tokens to indicate these roles. The raw tokenizers library has no concept of any of this.

The transformers library bridges this gap. The library is primarily known as a model definition library, but it also provides a tokenizer abstraction layer that wraps the raw tokenizers backend and adds model-aware functionality.

Here's the same tokenization with the transformers wrapper:

Notice how the special tokens like <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> are applied to the prompt before tokenizing. This is useful for the model to learn where a new sequence starts and ends.

The transformers tokenizer adds everything the raw library lacks:

transformers implements the tokenization API that is most commonly used in the entire ML community (encode, decode, convert_tokens_to_ids, etc.)

The transformers library organizes tokenizers into a class hierarchy. At the top sits a base class that defines the common interface. Below it, backend classes handle the actual tokenization using different engines. At the bottom, model-specific classes configure the backends for particular models.

PreTrainedTokenizerBase is the abstract base class for all tokenizers in transformers. It defines the interface that every tokenizer must implement.

The base class handles functionality that doesn't depend on the tokenization backend:

Every tokenizer in transformers ultimately inherits from PreTrainedTokenizerBase. The base class ensures consistent behavior across all tokenizers, regardless of which backend they use for the actual tokenization.

TokenizersBackend is the primary backend class for most modern tokenizers. It inherits from PreTrainedTokenizerBase and wraps the Rust-based tokenizers library.

The class stores the Rust tokenizer object internally:

When you call encoding methods on a TokenizersBackend tokenizer, the class delegates the actual tokenization to the Rust backend:

The Rust backend performs computationally intensive work, while the Python wrapper adds the model-aware features on top.

Many model-specific tokenizers inherit from TokenizersBackend, examples include:

These model-specific classes configure the backend with the correct vocabulary, merge rules, special tokens, and normalization settings for their respective models.

PythonBackend inherits from PreTrainedTokenizerBase and implements tokenization in pure Python. The class is aliased as PreTrainedTokenizer.

The pure-Python backend exists for several reasons:

The Python backend is slower than the Rust backend. For most use cases, the Rust-backed TokenizersBackend is preferred.

Model-specific tokenizers that inherit from PythonBackend (or its alias PreTrainedTokenizer) include some older or specialized models, like:

SentencePieceBackend inherits from PythonBackend and provides integration with Google's SentencePiece library. SentencePiece is a standalone tokenization library that many models use, particularly those trained by Google.

The backend wraps a SentencePiece processor:

Models that use SentencePiece tokenization inherit from this backend. Examples include:

The SentencePiece backend inherits from PythonBackend rather than directly from PreTrainedTokenizerBase because it shares much of the same interface and padding/truncation logic.

AutoTokenizer is the recommended entry point for loading tokenizers. It automatically determines which tokenizer class to use for a given model and returns an instance of that class.

Behind the scenes, AutoTokenizer performs these steps:

The benefit of AutoTokenizer is that you don't need to know which tokenizer class a model uses. Whether a model uses LlamaTokenizer, GPT2Tokenizer, or BertTokenizer, the same AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("model-name") call works.

The tokenizer system in transformers forms a layered architecture:

The most significant change in Transformers v5 is a philosophical shift in how tokenizers are defined. Tokenizers now work like PyTorch's nn.Module: you define the architecture first, then fill it with learned parameters.

In v4, tokenizers were black boxes tied to pretrained checkpoint files. If you loaded LlamaTokenizerFast, you couldn't easily answer basic questions about it:

The __init__ method gave no clues. You had to dig through serialized files or external documentation to understand what the tokenizer actually did.

v4 also maintained two parallel implementations for every model:

Worst of all, you couldn't create an empty tokenizer architecture. If you wanted to train a LLaMA-style tokenizer on your own data, there was no clean way to instantiate a "blank" LLaMA tokenizer and fill it with your vocabulary and merges. Tokenizers existed only as loaded checkpoints, not as configurable templates.

v5 treats tokenizer architecture (normalizer, pre-tokenizer, model type, post-processor, decoder) as distinct from trained parameters (vocabulary, merges). This mirrors how PyTorch separates model architecture from learned weights.

The tokenizer class now explicitly declares its structure. Looking at LlamaTokenizer in v5, you can immediately see:

This transparency was impossible in v4, where the same information was buried in serialized files.

v5 consolidates the two-file system into a single file per model. LlamaTokenizer now inherits from TokenizersBackend, which wraps the Rust-based tokenizer that was previously exposed as the “fast” implementation and is now the default.

The former “slow” Python implementation lives explicitly behind PythonBackend, and SentencePieceBackend remains for models that require it, but Rust-backed tokenization is the preferred default.

Users now have one clear entry point. Advanced users who need to customize can still access lower-level components, but the library no longer forces everyone to navigate two parallel implementations.

Suppose you want a tokenizer that behaves exactly like LLaMA's – same normalization, same pre-tokenization, same BPE model type – but trained on a domain-specific corpus (medical text, legal documents, a new language). In v4, this required manually reconstructing the tokenizer pipeline from low-level tokenizers library primitives. In v5, you can instantiate the architecture directly and call train:

The resulting tokenizer will have your custom vocabulary and merge rules, but will process text identically to how a standard LLaMA tokenizer would with the same whitespace handling, same special token conventions, same decoding behavior.

The shift from "tokenizers as loaded checkpoints" to "tokenizers as configurable architectures" makes the library more modular, more transparent, and more aligned with how practitioners think about building ML systems.

Transformers v5 brings three improvements to tokenization:

The wrapper layer between tokenizers and Transformers remains essential. It adds model awareness, context lengths, chat templates, special tokens, that raw tokenization doesn't provide. V5 just makes that layer clearer and more customizable.

If you are looking to learn more about tokenization here are some resources:

Experiment with and compare different tokenizers

I think it depends on the nature of tools

Thanks for doing this! I had to train some tokenizers with the v4, it was indeed not straightforward to understand the behavior.

#10205. Yes, government officials confirm, the Jensen Huang scandal is really, really bad

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has found himself embroiled in a scandal involving an alleged affair, a suspected Chinese spy, and some of America’s most closely guarded technology. Not exactly your garden-variety corporate indiscretion.

There’s a lot to worry about. Experts are concerned that Huang’s repeated calls to loosen restrictions on advanced chip exports to China may have been influenced by the relationship. The affair also raises questions about Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer led by Alice Huang. The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed last year, the New York Times reported, but transferred the probe to the Justice Department after Nvidia reached out.

One of the stranger twists in the still-unfolding scandal is that the Trump administration appears to have known about the relationship—and Alice Huang’s suspected ties to the Chinese government—for some time. Yet intelligence officials apparently never warned Jensen Huang, and Trump seems to be brushing off the scandal. Despite an FBI investigation, the president has called Nvidia’s CEO an “honorable guy” and says he believes Huang didn’t know Alice was a spy. Nvidia’s board, meanwhile, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised” and has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

But current and former government tech officials say the assurances from Trump and Nvidia’s board do little to dispel their concerns. “A sophisticated individual should not have fallen prey to these advances,” a senior government official who focuses on AI issues tells Fast Company.

“Obvious targets for espionage”

The concern extends beyond Jensen Huang’s call for U.S. regulators to clear advanced chips to China. It’s possible Alice Huang may have picked up classified information—anything Trump might have mentioned—from the Nvidia CEO, given his close relationship with the president, suggests David Nesting, a former White House AI and cybersecurity official. Alice Huang may have had access to Nvidia information, too. (CHIPS for America, the Commerce Department initiative overseeing federal investments in semiconductor manufacturing and research, did not respond to Fast Company’s request for comment.)

“His home, office, electronic devices, and private and professional communications would all be attractive intelligence targets,” Nesting tells Fast Company. “China would be enormously interested in Nvidia’s intellectual property, technology, roadmaps, supply chain, and how they might circumvent their export controls.”

People who have sensitive and classified information are supposed to protect that information, but also work with security officials and alert them to anyone who might be asking about it, says the senior government official. “This is not just personal foibles,” the official adds. “Nvidia’s power and integral role in AI means that all decisions made by Mr. Huang inure not only to Nvidia but to the AI industry.”

The affair, and its corresponding national security implications, underscore the risks of concentrating so much of the AI industry in the hands of a single company. Nvidia controls an estimated 80% of the market for GPUs used in AI, according to the OECD. That dependence has, in effect, exposed the country to an “enormous single point of failure,” argues Varoon Mathur, who formerly worked on AI issues at the White House.

“When so much depends on one company, that company and its leadership become obvious targets for espionage, coercion, and foreign interference,” he says.

“The wake-up call we all need”

Pamela Jennings, a former senior policy officer at the CHIPS Research and Development program, housed inside the National Institute of Standards and Technology, sees the immediate fallout as a corporate crisis for Nvidia’s board to address. But the scandal also raises broader questions about how the U.S. cultivates a more resilient tech sector.

“It’s kind of interesting to think about where we are in terms of—particularly in the U.S.—looking at innovation and how we are supporting and resourcing innovation,” Jennings says. “It’s not so much whether Nvidia has a lot of power or not a lot of power, but what feeds into those larger companies and branches from them to make us even more robust and more of a leader globally.”

For another former AI official at the Transportation Department, the scandal raises an even more fundamental concern: how much influence unelected technology executives wield over American foreign policy.

“We’ve handed the keys of international statecraft to CEOs who answer to no voter,” the official says. “The fact that one executive’s bedroom partner could impact worldwide AI and data sovereignty initiatives is the wake-up call we all need.”

The baying of the hounds can be heard at a distance. Yesterday, Nvidia's Jensen Huang confirmed that it was indeed true that he had a romantic affair with Alice Huang (not related to the family), who U.S. intelligence services claim is a Chinese honeypot tasked with facilitating smuggling of the firm's advanced GPUs into China. Now, a class-action lawsuit and investigations have started flying from almost everywhere.

This development is not unexpected, as basic securities law allows shareholders to sue their investees if they misrepresent facts or otherwise perform actions that cause a drop in stock prices. They may have a point, as Nvidia's shares dipped significantly when the confirmation of Jensen's infidelity and the ramifications thereof hit the press everywhere.

The legal proceedings are bound to be numerous, but as of right now, the first class-action lawsuit was filed by the Rosen Law Firm. The suit claims that Nvidia and Jensen Huang failed to disclose or misled investors regarding Jensen's affair with Alice, lied about it when asked, raised national security concerns, and caused a subsequent loss of Nvidia's reputation. You can check out the case docket at PacerMonitor here.

While legal analysis is beyond the scope of this news, Nvidia did downplay Jensen's relationship with Alice, saying that "Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year."

Other legal firms have launched their own investigations into the recent development, with essentially the same justification: Schall, Brown & Schwartz attributes a 5.5% pre-market-trading drop to Nvidia, as does Levi & Korsinsky. The office of Frank R. Cruz mentions an 8.8% figure related to intra-day exchanging, and is interested in shareholders with $50,000 in losses. The percentage-drop figure is 5.88% premarket for Bronstein, Gewritz & Grossman.

Every investigation and suit mentioned here requires no upfront fees from complainants, as with most class-action lawsuits. The underlying condition is often that the law firms involved get a cut of whichever damages or settlements may appear at the end of the lawsuit. Some of them, like the one by Levi & Korsinsky, even aim to relieve investors who've already sold their Nvidia shares and sold them at a loss, with no minimum amount required.

#10202. How ‘key person risk’ derails companies—and poses problems for Nvidia amid Jensen Huang scandal

When companies put all their faith and trust in one powerful leader, backup plans when things go south are hard to come by. Just ask Nvidia. The world’s second most valuable company (but as of today, the third) is currently in the throes of a major PR scandal that hasn’t just shaken trust in the tech company’s leader, but in the entire company.

Over the weekend, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Amid the controversy, the company announced it would launch an independent investigation of the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, an executive from the Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed, over reports that he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” 

As the company grapples with the controversy, and potential legal ramifications, concerns over the leader’s judgment loom large, especially given he’s been one of AI’s most vocal advocates and as China and the U.S. continue to battle it out to keep pace with one another in the AI race. While the company’s stock was trending down ahead of the midterm election, since the revelation, it’s been plummeting ever since. It now sits 22% below its October peak.

Turns out, there’s a phenomenon that explains the dangers of putting all your eggs in the basket of a single, all-powerful and important leader.

What is Key Man (or Person) Risk?

The ordeal is a prime example of something called key man (person) risk, which refers to when a company leans too heavily on one leader, making that leader’s own actions—their successes or failures—crucial for the entire company’s survival. That seems to be precisely the case for Nvidia, where Huang (a tech mastermind) has become, not just an asset, but utterly irreplaceable. That’s especially true because there is no clear successor for the powerful CEO.

As an analyst at Bernstein explained to Reuters, “Nvidia is not an ordinary company, and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he is Nvidia” and “clearly sets the long-term strategy and direction.”

Of course, all businesses have leaders—or maybe a few. But that doesn’t mean that companies should depend entirely on them for their most important connections, tasks, and undertakings all at once. According to Wright People PR, companies should seek to mitigate key person risk by cross-training employees, and focus on succession planning and team collaboration. 

Why the risk is growing

Still, as a handful of tech leaders become more and more powerful, key man risk seems to be accelerating. 

Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNN that it “has never been more of a blessing and a curse” than it is right now. 

“We’ve always had powerful CEOs but never in history have we been at a point where such an important industry is run by people you can count on two hands,” Ives explained.

In other words, it’s not just Huang and Nvidia who are exemplifying how to put all of your eggs in one basket. All of the largest tech companies and their single leaders—Meta’s Zuckerberg, Anthropic’s Amodei, Tesla and Space X’s Musk, and so on—are guilty.  That could mean that some of the most powerful companies are the most at risk. 

The phenomenon can also show up in politics, as it recently has come on full display following last week’s blue tsunami in the U.S. midterms: GOP leaders are increasingly backing away from President Donald Trump, as the Democrats’ blowout win highlights just how disillusioned they are with the policies of a Republican party that’s been remade in his image over the last decade.

As for Nvidia, the company is busy trying to downplay the controversy while surveying the damage. In a Nov. 8 press release, the company said, “The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” it said in a statement. 

It noted that the board “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”
