#10201. AprielGuard: A Guardrail for Safety and Adversarial Robustness in Modern LLM Systems

Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly evolved from text-only assistants into complex agentic systems capable of performing multi-step reasoning, calling external tools, retrieving memory, and executing code. With this evolution comes an increasingly sophisticated threat landscape: not only traditional content safety risks, but also multi-turn jailbreaks, prompt injections, memory hijacking, and tool manipulation.

In this work, we introduce AprielGuard, an 8B parameter safety–security safeguard model designed to detect:

AprielGuard is available in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, enabling explainable classification when needed and low-latency classification for production pipelines.

Traditional safety classifiers primarily focus on a limited classification spectrum (e.g., toxicity or self-harm), assume short inputs, and evaluate single user messages. Modern deployments, however, feature:

As a result, production teams increasingly rely on workarounds: multiple guard models for different stages, regex filters, static rules, or hand-crafted heuristics. These approaches are brittle and do not scale.

AprielGuard addresses these issues with a unified model and a unified safety + adversarial taxonomy, built specifically for modern LLM agent ecosystems.

AprielGuard operates across three input formats:

(These 16 categories are inspired from SALAD-Bench)

The model detects and evaluates a wide range of adversarial prompt patterns designed to manipulate model behavior or evade safety mechanisms. The model outputs a binary classification (e.g., adversarial / non_adversarial) rather than fine-grained attack categories.

The training data covers diverse adversarial types such as role-playing, world-building, persuasion, and stylization, among many other complex prompt manipulation strategies. These examples represent only a subset of the broader adversarial scenarios incorporated in the training data.

Synthetic data: AprielGuard is trained on a synthetically generated training dataset. The training data points are generated at a sub-topic level of the taxonomy for better coverage. We leverage Mixtral-8x7B and internally developed uncensored models to generate unsafe content for training purposes. Models were prompted with higher temperature to induce output variation. Prompting templates are meticulously tailored to ensure accurate data generation. Adversarial attacks are constructed using a combination of synthetic data points, diverse prompt templates, and rule-based generation techniques. We leveraged NVIDIA NeMo Curator to generate large-scale, multi-turn conversational datasets featuring complex, realistic scenarios with iterative and evolving attacks through context switches. This approach enabled us to systematically synthesize diverse interaction patterns, improving the robustness of the model to long-horizon reasoning, adversarial turns, and evolving user intent. We also used SyGra framework for synthetic data generation processes for harmful prompts and attacks generation. The training dataset encompasses diverse content formats such as conversational dialogues, forum posts, tweets, instructional prompts, questions, and how-to guides.

Data augmentation: To enhance model robustness, a range of data augmentation techniques were applied to the training data. These augmentations are designed to expose the model to natural variations and perturbations that commonly occur in real-world scenarios. Specifically, the dataset includes transformations such as character-level noise, insertion of typographical errors, leetspeak substitutions, word-level paraphrasing, and syntactic reordering. Such augmentations help the model generalize better by reducing sensitivity to superficial variations in input, thereby improving resilience against adversarial manipulations and non-standard text representations.

Agentic workflows: Agentic workflows represent real-world scenarios where autonomous agents execute multi-step tasks involving planning, reasoning, and interaction with tools, APIs, and other agents. These workflows often include sequences of user prompts, system messages, intermediate reasoning steps, and tool invocations, making them susceptible to diverse attack vectors. To construct these training data points, we synthetically generate a wide range of scenarios across multiple domains, capturing realistic agentic interactions between a user and an agentic system. Each data point is enriched with detailed contextual elements—including tool definitions, tool invocation logs, agent roles and policies, execution traces, conversation history, memory states, and scratch-pad reasoning. For malicious or adversarial examples, we corrupt the relevant segment of the workflow to reflect a specific attack vector. Depending on the scenario, this may involve modifying user prompts, altering intermediate reasoning traces, modifying the tool outputs, injecting false memory states, or disrupting inter-agent communication. By systematically perturbing different components of the agentic workflow, we produce high-fidelity examples that expose a model to a diverse spectrum of realistic and challenging attack patterns. Each data point was simulated to reflect realistic executions, incorporating both benign and adversarial sequences.

Long context use cases: We curated a specialized long context dataset composed of diverse, high-length use cases such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) work-flows, multi-turn conversational threads, incident details, and operational reports containing detailed communications. These examples simulate real-world environments where large text contexts are typical.

AprielGuard is built on top of an Apriel-1.5 Thinker Base variant, downscaled to an 8B configuration for efficient deployment.

AprielGuard performance on the public safety benchmarks.

A comparative assessment of model performance using aggregated results from safety benchmarks.

AprielGuard performance on the public adversarial benchmarks.

A comparative assessment of model performance using aggregated results from adversarial benchmarks.

We curated an internal benchmark dataset aimed at evaluating the detection of Safety Risks and Adversarial Attacks within agentic workflows. To construct this benchmark, we systematically designed multiple attack scenarios targeting different components of the workflow—such as prompt inputs, reasoning traces, tool parameters, memory states, and inter-agent communications. Each instance was annotated according to the taxonomy of vulnerabilities. Each workflow was simulated to reflect realistic executions, incorporating both benign and adversarial sequences. The dataset captures granular attack points across various stages such as planning, reasoning, execution, and response generation to provide fine-grained evaluation of model robustness. Overall, the dataset comprises a balanced mixture of safety risks and adversarial attacks.

Safety performance of different models on the agentic benchmark.

Adversarial performance of different models on the agentic benchmark..

Many real world safety or adversarial risks do not manifest in short, isolated text snippets, but rather emerge across use cases such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflows, multi-turn conversational threads, organizational incident details, and operational reports containing detailed communications. A guardian model must therefore detect subtle or "needle-in-a-haystack" cases, where malicious or manipulative content is sparsely distributed, embedded across multiple references, or intentionally obscured within benign text.

To evaluate AprielGuard’s long-context reasoning capabilities, we curated a specialized test dataset composed of diverse, high-length use cases. We considered the data upto 32k tokens for this evaluation. The baseline data was initially constructed from benign content representative of these domains. Malicious elements were then systematically injected to simulate adversarial or unsafe scenarios while maintaining the overall coherence of the text. For example, in an incident case summarization, an injection could be embedded within the case description, hidden in a metadata section, or inserted as part of a comment thread. Similarly, in multi-turn dialogue data, adversarial content might appear mid-conversation, near the end or at the beginning to test long range dependency tracking.

A major limitation in the current landscape of content moderation research is the scarcity of high- quality multilingual benchmarks. To address this gap and comprehensively assess the multilingual capabilities of AprielGuard, we extended the Safety Risks benchmarks and Adversarial Attack benchmarks into multiple non-English languages. The translation process was conducted using the MADLAD400-3B-MT model, a multilingual machine translation model based on the T5 architecture.

For this study, we selected eight of the most widely used non-English languages to ensure broad linguistic and geographical coverage: French, French-Canadian, German, Japanese, Dutch, Spanish, Portuguese-Brazilian, and Italian. Each instance from the English Safety and Adversarial benchmarks was translated into the eight target languages. During translation, we preserved the original English role identifiers, such as User: and Assistant:, while translating only the conversational content. This design choice ensures alignment with AprielGuard’s moderation framework, where the role context plays a crucial part in evaluating safety and adversarial intent.

As LLMs move toward deeply integrated agentic systems, the need for unified pipelines becomes more critical. AprielGuard is a step toward that future — reducing complexity, improving coverage, and offering a scalable foundation for trustworthy AI deployments.

Language Coverage: While AprielGuard has been primarily trained on English data, limited testing indicates it performs reasonably well across several languages, including: English, German, Spanish, French, French (Canada), Italian, Dutch, and Portuguese (Brazil). However, thorough testing and calibration are strongly recommended before deploying the model for production use in non-English settings.

Adversarial Robustness: Despite targeted training on adversarial and manipulative behaviors, the model may still exhibit vulnerability to complex or unseen attack strategies.

Domain Sensitivity: AprielGuard may underperform on highly specialized or technical domains (e.g., legal, medical, or scientific contexts) that require nuanced contextual understanding.

Latency–Interpretability Trade-off: Enabling reasoning traces enhances explainability but increases latency and compute cost. For low-latency or large-scale use cases, non-reasoning mode is recommended.

Reasoning Mode Sensitivity: The model exhibits occasional inconsistencies in classification outcomes between reasoning-enabled and non-reasoning inference modes.

Intended use: AprielGuard is intended strictly for use as a safeguard and risk assessment model. It classifies potential safety risks and adversarial threats according to the AprielGuard unified taxonomy. Any deviation from the prescribed inference may lead to unintended, unsafe, or unreliable behavior.

#10200. A viral TikTok trend is turning ordinary photos into something unexpectedly emotional

Looking back through old photographs often happens in a family living room, turning the pages of a loved one’s photo albums. But on TikTok, the nostalgic ritual is its own trend, and it’s set to the tune of Pink Floyd.

In a new trend on TikTok, users are showcasing their life progress by looking back to their childhood, comparing their baby photos to recent ones. While the captions vary across videos, it’s the music and lyrics that brings all of them together: Pink Floyd’s Time.

The trend uses the photo-carousel feature on TikTok as a template: the first photo is of the user at a young age, with the next one being a recent image. The first photograph has the beginning of one of the song’s lines typed on it, “The sun is the same, in a relative way,” followed by the “but you are older,” written in the recent photo.

For many users, the trend is a way to show that, despite years passed, key attributes of the user remain the same. Take content creator Eugenia McQuarrie, who posted a photo of herself at a beauty salon, with rollers in her hair. The photo is followed by a present day image of McQuarrie, wearing hair rollers as an adult.

A user replied saying, “diva since day one.”

Another user had a similar take on the trend, first posting a photo of himself as a kid, wearing a firefighter toy hat, cutting to his grown up version wearing a real-life firefighter uniform.

The trend has quickly gained momentum on the platform, with over 8.8 million views in the span of weeks, according to trend-tracking agency Masterhooks.

Part of the appeal is the trend’s versatility, allowing users to make it their own, turning to videos and edits, keeping only the soundtrack.

Sometimes it was the small mannerisms that remained unchanged by time, which users wanted to highlight. Like one user who first shows a video of her dancing as a kid in her living room, then cuts to her dancing at a party as an adult.

“Still the same vibe, how cute,” one user commented.

For others, nostalgia didn’t reach as far back as most. Ballet content creator Katelyn Power, for instance, posted a video of her dancing ballet four years earlier, cut to her most recent performance of the same dance.

A user commented, “Pink Floyd and ballet? I am in heaven.”

As reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. Historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting big on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

An Oslo rooftop, about 80 watts, and a hand-aimed antenna were enough to reach orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Oslo radio amateur group, working with Tanagra Space, got a European Space Agency satellite to recognize and launch the 1993 game Doom after catching the word in a voice command sent over the 23 cm band. It took seven attempts, shared with a group in Poland, and the command finally got through on the last two, on the same day in late July. The satellite “understood its assignment,” with the help of a matcher after the 27 MB onboard speech model transcribed the audio, returning a postcard with details of the launch.

The satellite, named OPS-SAT PRETTY and flying under the ESA’s OPS-SAT Space Lab program for outside experiments, ran the game in an experiment punningly called PRETTY DOOMed. Doom ran on a different satellite, the OPS-SAT-1, in 2023, but this time is different, as the game was launched with a voice command.

The radio club sending the command in question is LA4O, of the Norwegian Radio Relay League, hams transmitting as part of the experiment. The club’s signal went over 1296 MHz narrowband FM at about 80 W, indicated, using an Icom IC-9700 radio and a Wimo helix antenna at 15.1 dBi, directed by hand. As for the voice, Run 6, the morning pass, used a looped synthesized voice from a keyer, with three of six captures detecting the command. Run 7, the evening pass, used a live operator at a microphone, with one of five usable captures detecting it.

The live operator’s command was “LIMA ALFA FOUR OSCAR, PRETTY PLAY DOOM DOOM DOOM, PRETTY PLAY DOOM DOOM DOOM.” The call sign is for legal identification.

On board the satellite, the voice is transcribed by a 27 MB quantized English speech-recognition model, picked because it could fit the satellite’s limited computer. The voice was handled by software-defined radio (SDR), which was able to narrow in on the voice and demodulate the source for the speech model. Tuning and demodulating a signal is usually handled by fixed circuits, but using software has the advantage of being mutable with an uploaded update. The voice used this time “was only the test signal,” project lead Georges Labrèche said, and the same setup could handle other things with a new model.

The live-voice transcript caught “AND FAR BRIEFLY PLAYING DOOM STEAM DOOM PRECIPATED” with two exact DOOM matches, although one DOOM is enough. Morning detections passed only on fuzzy tolerance with transcripts such as “PLAY DOON.” The achievement is less on the understood side and more about differentiating a voice and a specific command out of the noise in orbit.

This can be an iffy business, which is one reason it took seven runs, and being able to update proved useful. The spacecraft heard LA4O, but the output was mostly static, because about 170 kHz reached the FM discriminator for a signal of about ±5 kHz. Offline analysis brought a fix: find the peak within ±100 kHz, shift to baseband, low-pass, and decimate before demodulation. It’s effectively like tuning a car radio to a specific station.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Tanagra then reproduced the fix and was able to remove a redundant audio filter. Delivery of the fix took about a week, although the Oslo group’s effort took 59 days and about 7,200 NOK (about $770), pizza included.

Tanagra proposes repeat runs that keep the original data and send it back down to Earth, so the researchers can test the live-voice result properly. Better detection may be possible with larger speech models, too, which the team could test on the ground first. Labrèche says the team has demonstrated “a satellite that can listen to any type of radio signal.” Hopefully, the setup can one day detect “mayday” calls and even radio bursts from space.

Today at CES 2026, NVIDIA unveiled a world of new open models to enable the future of agents, online and in the real world. From the recently released NVIDIA Nemotron reasoning LLMs to the new NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1.6 open reasoning VLA and NVIDIA Cosmos world foundation models, all the building blocks are here today for AI Builders to build their own agents.

But what if you could bring your own agent to life, right at your desk? An AI buddy that can be useful to you and process your data privately?

In the CES keynote today, Jensen Huang showed us how we can do exactly that, using the processing power of NVIDIA DGX Spark with Reachy Mini to create your own little office R2D2 you can talk to and collaborate with.

This blog post provides a step-by-step guide to replicate this amazing experience at home using a DGX Spark and Reachy Mini.

If you want to start cooking right away, here’s the source code of the demo.

Feel free to adapt the recipe and make it your own - you have many ways to integrate the models into your application:

Turning an AI agent from a simple chat interface into something you can interact with naturally makes conversations feel more real. When an AI agent can see through a camera, speak out loud, and perform actions, the experience becomes more engaging. That’s what Reachy Mini makes possible.

Reachy Mini is designed to be customizable. With access to sensors, actuators, and APIs, you can easily wire it into your existing agent stack, by simulation or real hardware controlled directly from Python.

This post focuses on composing existing building blocks rather than reinventing them. We combine open models for reasoning and vision, an agent framework for orchestration, and tool handlers for actions. Each component is loosely coupled, making it easy to swap models, change routing logic, or add new behaviors.

Unlike closed personal assistants, this setup stays fully open. You control the models, the prompts, the tools, and the robot’s actions. Reachy Mini simply becomes the physical endpoint of your agent where perception, reasoning, and action come together.

In this example, we use the NVIDIA NeMo Agent Toolkit, a flexible, lightweight, framework-agnostic open source library, to connect all the components of the agent together. It works seamlessly with other agentic frameworks, like LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, handling how models interact, routing inputs and outputs between them, and making it easy to experiment with different configurations or add new capabilities without rewriting core logic. The toolkit also provides built-in profiling and optimization features, letting you track token usage efficiency and latency across tools and agents, identify bottlenecks, and automatically tune hyperparameters to maximize accuracy while reducing cost and latency.

First, clone the repository that contains all the code you’ll need to follow along:

To access your intelligence layer, powered by the NVIDIA Nemotron models, you can either deploy them using NVIDIA NIM or vLLM, or connect to them through remote endpoints available at build.nvidia.com.

The following instructions assume you are accessing the Nemotron models via endpoints. Create a .env file in the main directory with your API keys. For local deployments, you do not need to specify API keys and can skip this step.

Start by getting a basic LLM chat workflow running through NeMo Agent Toolkit’s API server. NeMo Agent Toolkit supports running workflows via `nat serve` and providing a config file. The config file passed here contains all the necessary setup information for the agent, which includes the models used for chat, image understanding, as well as the router model used by the agent. The NeMo Agent Toolkit UI can connect over HTTP/WebSocket so you can chat with your workflow like a standard chat product. In this implementation, the NeMo Agent Toolkit server is launched on port 8001 (so your bot can call it, and the UI can too):

Next, verify that you can send a plain text prompt through a separate terminal to ensure everything is setup correctly:

Reviewing the agent configuration, you’ll notice it defines far more capabilities than a simple chat completion. The next steps will walk through those details.

Tool calling is an essential part of AI agents. NeMo Agent Toolkit includes a built-in ReAct agent that can reason between tool calls and use multiple tools before answering. We route “action requests” to a ReAct agent that’s allowed to call tools (for example, tools that trigger robot behaviors or fetch current robot state).

Take a look at this portion of the config it defines the tools (like Wikipedia search) and specifies the ReAct agent pattern used to manage them.

The key idea: don’t use one model for everything. Instead, route based on intent:

You can implement routing a few ways (heuristics, a lightweight classifier, or a dedicated routing service). If you want the “production” version of this idea, the NVIDIA LLM Router developer example is the full reference implementation and includes evaluation and monitoring patterns.

A basic routing policy might work like this:

These sections of the config define the routing topology and specify the router model.

NOTE: If you want to reduce latency/cost or run offline, you can self-host one of the routed models (typically the “fast text” model) and keep the VLM remote. One common approach is serving via NVIDIA NIM or vLLM and pointing NeMo Agent Toolkit to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Now we go real time. Pipecat is a framework designed for low-latency voice/multimodal agents: it orchestrates audio/video streams, AI services, and transports so you can build natural conversations. In this repo, the bot service is responsible for:

You will find all the pipecat bot code in the `reachy-personal-assistant/bot` folder.

Reachy Mini exposes a daemon that the rest of your system connects to. The repo runs the daemon in simulation by default (--sim). If you have access to a real Reachy you can remove this flag and the same code will control your robot.

You will need three terminals to run the entire system:

If you are using the physical hardware, remember to omit the --sim flag from the command.

If the NeMo Agent Toolkit service is not already running from Step 1, start it now in Terminal 3.

Once all the terminals are set up, there are two main windows to keep track of:

Reachy Sim – This window appears automatically when you start the simulator daemon in Terminal 1. This is applicable if you’re running Reachy mini simulation in place of the physical device.

Pipecat Playground – This is the client-side UI where you can connect to the agent, enable microphone and camera inputs, and view live transcripts. In Terminal 2, open the URL exposed by the bot service: http://localhost:7860/. Click “CONNECT” in your browser. It may take a few seconds to initialize, and you’ll be prompted to grant microphone (and optionally camera) access.

At this point, you can start interacting with your agent!

Here are a few simple prompts to help you test your personal assistant. You can start with these and then experiment by adding your own to see how the agent responds!

Text-only prompts (routes to the fast text model)

You've finished building your website. The HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files are ready, everything works locally, and now you need somewhere to publish it.

Static website hosting is one of the simplest ways to get a website online. Many providers offer free plans, and you don't need to maintain a traditional web server.

The harder part is choosing the right provider. Some let you upload a single HTML file and share it immediately. Others connect to GitHub, automatically deploy code changes, and support entire development teams.

We've compared eight static hosting providers, including TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel, and GitHub Pages. Below, you'll find their free hosting limits, pricing, advantages, and drawbacks, along with recommendations for different types of projects.

Static website hosting is a service that stores and delivers pre-built website files, including HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and fonts.

Unlike traditional server-rendered websites, static sites don't need a server to generate each page when someone visits. The HTML is already prepared and can be delivered directly to the visitor's browser.

That doesn't mean static websites can't be interactive. JavaScript can still handle navigation, forms, filtering, and other features. Static sites can also communicate with external APIs or databases.

The main distinction is how pages are generated.

You can write a static website using plain HTML or generate one with frameworks and tools such as Astro, Hugo, Eleventy, or Next.js static export.

Static hosting is also commonly associated with Jamstack, an approach that separates the front end from back-end services.

Lower hosting costs: Many providers let you publish smaller websites for free.

Simpler maintenance: There's no application server or server-side runtime to maintain for the static pages themselves.

Efficient content delivery: Static files can be cached across a content delivery network (CDN), reducing the distance between visitors and website assets.

There are limitations, too. If your website requires user authentication, database operations, or server-side functionality, you'll need additional services or a hosting platform that supports them.

We compared eight providers based on their deployment methods, free plan allowances, pricing, and suitability for different projects.

Free hosting limits: Bandwidth, storage, build allowances, and restrictions.

Deployment process: Whether you can upload files directly or need a Git repository.

Custom domains and HTTPS: Support for publishing under your own domain.

Development features: Automatic deployments, preview environments, and integrations.

Pricing: What happens when a project exceeds its free allowance.

Usage restrictions: Whether free hosting is suitable for commercial projects.

The following table summarizes the main differences between all eight services.

Free plans aren't directly comparable. For example, Vercel restricts its Hobby plan to personal, non-commercial use, while GitHub Pages prohibits using the service as free hosting for an online business or commercial SaaS.

Bandwidth limits also aren't the same as visitor limits. A website serving large images or downloadable files can consume its monthly allowance with relatively few visitors.

Cloudflare Pages is a strong choice for developers who want to host static websites without worrying about a conventional monthly bandwidth cap.

You can connect a GitHub or GitLab repository, and Cloudflare automatically builds and deploys the website when you push changes. Direct uploads are also supported.

A maximum individual file size of 25 MiB.

The combination is useful for blogs, documentation websites, and other projects that primarily serve HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images.

Cloudflare also provides preview deployments, custom domains, and HTTPS support.

No fixed bandwidth cap for static asset delivery.

Generous free plan for typical static websites.

Monthly build limits can matter for frequently updated projects.

Cloudflare's product range can make the initial setup less straightforward for beginners.

Cloudflare is increasingly emphasizing Workers Static Assets for new projects. Pages remains available, but developers starting a new application should compare both deployment approaches.

For a conventional static website, however, Pages is still a practical option, particularly when traffic could grow beyond the limits of other free plans.

See the official Cloudflare Pages limits for the current allowances.

Netlify combines static website hosting with tools designed to make development and deployment easier.

Connect a Git repository, configure your build settings, and Netlify can publish a new version whenever you push changes.

It also creates deploy previews, allowing you to inspect changes before merging them into your production branch.

This is useful when multiple people work on the same website or when you want to review design changes before publishing.

Netlify supports custom domains, HTTPS, serverless functions, and form handling.

Netlify's free plan uses a credit-based model with 300 credits per month.

Production deployments consume 15 credits each.

Web requests consume 2 credits per 10,000 requests.

Deploy previews and branch deployments consume no deployment credits.

The paid Personal plan starts at $9 per month and includes 1,000 monthly credits.

Convenient Git integration and deploy previews.

Built-in features such as forms and serverless functions.

Suitable for both simple websites and more advanced front-end projects.

Credit-based pricing requires monitoring several types of usage.

A busy site with frequent deployments can consume its free allowance faster than expected.

When comparing Netlify alternatives, Cloudflare Pages is particularly worth considering if your main concern is bandwidth.

For developers choosing between Vercel vs Netlify, the deciding factor is often the framework and workflow. Netlify offers a flexible approach to static site deployment, while Vercel has particularly close integration with Next.js.

Vercel is particularly well suited to Next.js applications, although it also supports React, Vue, Svelte, Astro, and other frameworks.

Like Netlify, Vercel connects to your Git repository and deploys updates automatically.

Every deployment receives its own URL, which helps developers review changes before publishing them to the main website.

Vercel also supports server-side rendering, functions, and other features beyond traditional static site hosting.

There is one important restriction: Vercel Hobby is intended for personal, non-commercial use only.

If you're deploying a business website or another commercial project, you'll need an appropriate paid plan.

Convenient deployment workflow for Next.js.

Supports both static and server-rendered applications.

Paid usage can involve multiple resource-based charges.

If you're building a personal Next.js application, Vercel is an obvious candidate. For a basic HTML website, however, its additional framework features may be unnecessary.

GitHub Pages is a straightforward way to publish a website directly from a GitHub repository.

It works particularly well for developer portfolios, project documentation, open-source websites, and small informational sites.

You can upload HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files to a repository, configure GitHub Pages, and publish them under a github.io subdomain.

GitHub Pages can serve existing static files or build websites using supported workflows, including Jekyll and GitHub Actions.

Published websites have a maximum size of 1 GB.

Bandwidth has a soft limit of 100 GB per month.

Free accounts can publish Pages sites from public repositories.

The bandwidth and build restrictions are soft limits, meaning they aren't necessarily enforced as strict cutoffs.

Simple integration with GitHub repositories.

Well suited to documentation and open-source projects.

Free accounts require a public repository for Pages.

GitHub Pages is not intended for running online businesses, e-commerce websites, or commercial SaaS products.

GitHub Pages is particularly convenient if your code already lives on GitHub and you only need to publish documentation or a portfolio.

For commercial websites, Cloudflare Pages or Netlify may be more appropriate.

The GitHub Pages documentation explains its hosting limits and usage restrictions.

Not every website needs a repository, deployment pipeline, or command-line interface.

If you've created a simple HTML page and want to share it, TiinyHost lets you upload an HTML file or ZIP archive and publish it under a shareable URL.

It can also host PDFs, making it useful for sharing documents and presentations alongside website projects.

The main advantage is the upload process. You don't need to configure a repository or install development tools before publishing.

Sharing an HTML file with someone who doesn't use Git.

The free plan includes one active site, a 3 MB project upload limit, and an allowance of 5,000 monthly visits.

The Tiny plan costs €5 per month when billed monthly. It supports uploads up to 25 MB and includes built-in analytics.

The Solo plan starts at €13 per month when billed monthly and adds features such as custom domains, password protection, and additional projects.

Annual billing is available at lower effective monthly prices.

No Git repository or command line required.

Suitable for previews and smaller projects.

The free plan's 3 MB limit is restrictive for websites with many images or other assets.

Custom domains require the Solo plan or higher.

Upload-based publishing is less convenient than Git automation for frequently updated websites.

For someone who simply needs free HTML hosting to share a small project, TiinyHost is worth considering.

For a larger production website that receives regular updates, Git-based hosting is likely to be more manageable.

Firebase Hosting is Google's hosting service for static websites and web application assets.

It integrates with other Firebase products, including Authentication, Cloud Firestore, and Cloud Functions.

That makes it useful when a website needs static hosting but also relies on Google's back-end services.

Deployment is handled through the Firebase command-line interface.

After configuring your project, you can deploy using:

Firebase distributes website assets through its CDN and supports custom domains with SSL certificates.

The Blaze plan uses pay-as-you-go billing while retaining applicable no-cost allowances.

One detail worth checking is the distinction between Firebase Hosting and Firebase App Hosting. They are separate products with different features and pricing models.

Integrates with Firebase Authentication and Firestore.

Useful for applications already using Google's developer services.

Initial setup is more involved than uploading an HTML file.

The daily transfer allowance may become restrictive for larger websites.

Firebase Hosting makes the most sense when Firebase is already part of your application.

For a standalone static blog or portfolio that doesn't use Firebase services, Cloudflare Pages or GitHub Pages may be simpler.

Amazon S3 and CloudFront offer a different approach to static hosting.

Instead of using a platform that handles the entire deployment process, you combine AWS services to store and deliver your website.

S3 stores the website files, while CloudFront distributes them through a CDN.

This setup provides control over caching, permissions, security, and integration with other AWS services.

It can be suitable for organizations already using AWS or developers who need specific infrastructure configurations.

AWS uses usage-based pricing for S3 storage, requests, and applicable CloudFront usage.

Free allowances may apply depending on your account and the current AWS pricing program, but you should calculate costs based on your expected traffic, storage, and requests.

Unlike simpler hosting services, there isn't one fixed monthly price for every website.

Several services can contribute to the final bill.

Incorrect permissions or origin settings can cause access errors.

One common issue when setting up S3 static website hosting is receiving a 403 Forbidden error because of bucket permissions or CloudFront origin configuration.

AWS recommends using CloudFront Origin Access Control with a regular S3 bucket origin so that the bucket can remain private. This differs from exposing the S3 website endpoint directly, which does not support HTTPS on its own.

AWS S3 and CloudFront are worth considering if you need that level of control. For a small static website, a managed hosting platform usually requires less setup.

Render is a cloud platform that supports static websites alongside web services, databases, background workers, and other application components.

Its static hosting works through a Git repository.

Connect your repository, select the build command and publish directory, and Render automatically deploys your website.

The service includes CDN delivery, custom domains, and managed TLS certificates.

Render is particularly useful when your project includes both a static front end and back-end services that you want to manage through the same platform.

Render's Hobby workspace is free and includes:

500 standard build pipeline minutes per month.

Additional bandwidth is billed at $0.15 per GB under the current pricing structure, so the Hobby workspace should not be treated as unlimited free hosting.

The Pro workspace costs $25 per month, excluding any applicable usage-based compute charges.

Static websites and back-end services on one platform.

The 5 GB included bandwidth allowance is relatively small.

Render makes sense when you're already using it for other parts of an application.

If you only need to host a static HTML website, Cloudflare Pages offers a more generous bandwidth allowance without the additional platform complexity.

Free static website hosting can be sufficient for a personal portfolio, documentation site, prototype, or small informational website.

However, the restrictions vary considerably between providers.

Some hosts measure data transfer, while others use visitor counts or a credit system. Check how each provider calculates usage rather than comparing headline numbers alone.

If your website rebuilds whenever you publish content, deployment limits matter. A blog updated a few times a month has different requirements from an application receiving dozens of deployments every day.

Free hosting doesn't always mean you can run a business website. Vercel's Hobby plan and GitHub Pages have restrictions that may rule out certain commercial projects.

Some services include custom domains on free plans. Others require an upgrade before you can connect one.

A free plan might stop serving additional usage, while another provider may bill for overages.

Before publishing a production website, check the provider's billing behavior and configure spending controls where available.

The right service depends primarily on how you build your website and what you intend to do with it.

For most developers publishing a conventional static website, Cloudflare Pages is a reasonable starting point.

If you're working with Git and want convenient previews and deployment tools, Netlify is another good choice.

For small files, temporary demos, and client previews, a simpler upload-based service may save time.

You should also consider how often the website will change.

Uploading files manually may be fine for a page that rarely changes. For a website with regular content updates, automated deployments from Git will generally be easier to maintain.

Publishing your website is only the first step. If you want search engines to discover and understand your pages, check the technical SEO basics before sharing the URL.

Every important page should have a descriptive HTML title and a relevant meta description.

You can use the Meta Tags Generator to create the necessary markup.

Open Graph tags help control how a page appears when shared on platforms that support them.

Set the title, description, canonical page URL where appropriate, and preview image.

A robots.txt file tells compliant crawlers which paths they may access. It doesn't guarantee indexing or prevent a public page from appearing in search results.

Use the Robots.txt Generator to create your crawler rules.

Include a sitemap with the canonical URLs you want search engines to discover.

Structured data helps search engines interpret eligible content.

Depending on the website, you may want Organization, Article, BreadcrumbList, or other relevant schema types.

The JSON-LD Schema Generator can help generate markup.

Confirm the correct domain loads over HTTPS.

Check canonical tags and redirect behavior.

Make sure important pages don't contain unintended noindex directives.

Test page performance and Core Web Vitals.

Verify the website in Google Search Console.

Static hosting makes serving website files relatively straightforward, but technical SEO still requires configuration and testing.

Cloudflare Pages is a good general-purpose choice because of its free static asset bandwidth and Git integration. Netlify is well suited to teams that need deploy previews, while GitHub Pages works well for portfolios and documentation. The best option depends on your deployment workflow, traffic requirements, and whether the website is commercial.

Yes. TiinyHost, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Firebase Hosting, Render, and several other services offer free hosting options. Most free plans have restrictions involving bandwidth, deployments, storage, or usage. Check the terms before using a free plan for a business website.

A small static website can cost nothing to host if it stays within a provider's free allowances. Paid plans vary from fixed monthly subscriptions to usage-based pricing. Domain registration, paid back-end services, and additional storage or bandwidth may increase the total cost.

For a standalone HTML file, upload-based hosting is generally the simplest approach. Services such as TiinyHost let you publish a file without configuring Git or a build process. If the project already lives in a GitHub repository, GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages may be more convenient.

GitHub Pages is a sensible option for documentation, open-source projects, and personal portfolios. Netlify offers more deployment features, including preview environments, forms, and functions. It also supports commercial projects, making it more appropriate for some business websites that would fall outside GitHub Pages' permitted uses.

Static website hosting doesn't need to be expensive or complicated. The important part is choosing a service that matches your website and deployment process.

Cloudflare Pages is a good starting point for static websites that need generous free bandwidth. Netlify is useful for Git-based development, while GitHub Pages suits personal projects and documentation.

If you're publishing a small HTML file or sharing a prototype, upload-based hosting may be all you need.

#10193. Failure Is Part of Entrepreneurship. These 5 Lessons Will Help You Recover.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Most businesses stumble at some point. How you respond decides whether the failure becomes a setback or a turning point, and the research has some useful pointers.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In 1989, I opened an Italian restaurant in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, where the waiters sang opera arias between courses. It was a lot of fun, but it was not a good business, and it closed in 1993.

I had assumed running a restaurant was easy. It isn’t. The location was wrong, the costs were too high, and I didn’t know the trade well enough to see either problem early. Around the same time, I put money into film production and property. Both businesses struggled and were sold in the mid-1990s.

I share this because founders tend to talk about their successes and quietly bury the rest. Yet failure is a normal part of business. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, only about half of new U.S. business establishments are still operating five years later. Hong Kong is no different. In 2025, a record number of companies registered in the city, but the South China Morning Post reported that more than 99,000 were dissolved in the same year.

Here are five lessons I have learned about failing — and about recovering.

Most of my early setbacks came from businesses I entered because they looked exciting, not because I understood them. The pattern is common. CB Insights’ 2026 analysis of startup shutdowns found that 43% cited poor product-market fit. I suspect many of those founders were very capable. They had simply misread a market they didn’t know well enough.

My rule since then has been simple: Never set up a business you don’t know. If you want to enter an unfamiliar field, partner with someone who has spent years in it, and listen to them.

The hardest decision in a struggling business is often the decision to stop. CB Insights found that 70% of failed startups ultimately ran out of capital, but running out of money is usually the last symptom, not the cause. By the time the bank balance forces your hand, months or even years may have been lost.

The same analysis, as reported by Crowdfund Insider, found that nearly a quarter of these companies had been “walking dead” for three years or more after their last funding round, still operating but no longer really growing. Hanging on rarely saves a business. More often, it makes the eventual decision more expensive.

Selling the film and property businesses was painful, but it freed up time, money and attention for something better. Closing a venture is not the same as failing as a person.

Losing a business can feel like a bereavement, and research suggests we should treat it as one. Professor Dean Shepherd’s work on grief and business failure, published in the Academy of Management Review, argues that founders recover and learn faster when they move between confronting the loss and stepping away from it, rather than dwelling on it or pretending it never happened.

The emotional cost is real. In a study of 242 entrepreneurs led by Dr. Michael Freeman of the University of California, San Francisco, 72% reported being affected by mental health conditions, either directly or through their families. Talk to someone you trust, sleep properly and keep exercising. You need a clear head to make your next decision well.

I learned to look after myself early. My father died when I was 18, aged just 49, and it made me take my health seriously long before it was fashionable. In difficult periods in business, that habit has helped keep me steady.

Experience alone does not make you a better founder. Harvard research by Paul Gompers and colleagues found that venture-backed entrepreneurs whose previous company had failed had a 20% chance of success next time, barely above the 18% for first-time founders. Those who had succeeded before had a 30% chance.

It also helps to know what kind of failure you are dealing with. In her book Right Kind of Wrong, Harvard Business School professor Amy Edmondson separates basic failures, caused by avoidable mistakes, from “intelligent failures,” which happen when you test a sensible idea in new territory and keep the downside small. The first kind should be prevented. The second is the price of progress.

The lessons don’t arrive by themselves. After a setback, I now write down what I assumed, what actually happened and what I would do differently, then ask someone outside the business to challenge it. Early in a career, a setback can feel like a judgment on your ability. With practice, it becomes a source of information.

A 2019 study in Nature by Yian Yin, Dashun Wang and colleagues analyzed more than 58,000 venture-backed startups, alongside other fields. People who eventually succeeded did not fail less often than those who didn’t. The difference was that each new attempt came faster, because they built on what they had already learned instead of starting from scratch. Speed here does not mean recklessness. It means shortening the gap between learning a lesson and acting on it.

That takes courage. The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor’s 2025/2026 report found that fear of failure deters two in five adults from starting a business. It also found that people who have previously exited a business are more likely to start again.

As I once told an interviewer, all these failures are what have shaped me. If you are recovering from one now, be patient with yourself, be honest about what went wrong, and, when you are ready, go again.

In 1989, I opened an Italian restaurant in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, where the waiters sang opera arias between courses. It was a lot of fun, but it was not a good business, and it closed in 1993.

I had assumed running a restaurant was easy. It isn’t. The location was wrong, the costs were too high, and I didn’t know the trade well enough to see either problem early. Around the same time, I put money into film production and property. Both businesses struggled and were sold in the mid-1990s.

I share this because founders tend to talk about their successes and quietly bury the rest. Yet failure is a normal part of business. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, only about half of new U.S. business establishments are still operating five years later. Hong Kong is no different. In 2025, a record number of companies registered in the city, but the South China Morning Post reported that more than 99,000 were dissolved in the same year.

Backend infrastructure failures included hardcoded, user-visible administrator credentials.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Before proceeding further, we'd like to advise our dear reader to sit down and perhaps grab a helmet, for this post will elicit quite a few face-palms and forehead-slaps. Two security researchers joined forces and, during early 2026, managed to hack the vehicle connectivity backend infrastructure of two automakers, managing to remotely open the doors on any of their net-connected cars and start their engines across multiple world regions.

The vulnerabilities were quickly fixed, and they pertained to a handful of belief-begging security issues with multiple server APIs that their respective mobile applications use. Furthermore, although remotely opening the cars and starting them were the most concerning bits, the vulnerabilities also exposed the vehicles' location, mileage, fuel, range, door states, and the customers' personal information.

The white-hat hacking duo isn't disclosing the name of the impacted automakers, but they managed to get access to Automaker #1's U.S. vehicles, while vehicles from Automaker #2 were susceptible to unplanned lock disengagement in Australia, the U.S., and Canada. As far as we can tell by visual inspection alone, the second firm may be Toyota, as the hack demonstration video appears to depict a RAV4 SUV.

Both affected automakers use ForgeRock's authentication and authorization services, though with the one small exception, the vulnerabilities found by Shubham Shah and Sam Curry pertained to poor implementations and security practices. One of their writeups goes over the ForgeRock-related affairs in detail for both companies, while Shah's article discusses the specifics on automaker #2 and their Australian connected-car infrastructure.

Shah first decompiled the company's Android application and found network calls to a telematics subdomain, quickly finding an "admintool" location containing a "TEST HARNESS" page with a login prompt. If you haven't been keeping track by now, the first problem is that this endpoint is reachable from the internet at large. But what really piqued Shah's interest was problem #2: a bundle of JavaScript code that should have been stripped of any unnecessary cruft actually contained the code for the backend's entire functionality, providing a map for further shenanigans.

This alone was enough to grant Shah the ability to pull up customer information with API keys that were hard-coded into said JavaScript. After some careful chaining of requests and connecting a license plate to a VIN with publicly available info, he connected that to a customer and found their email. At this point, the team noticed that the automaker was using ForgeRock's authentication mechanisms, and spent "a couple weeks" finding how they were used.

And this is also where they assess that the easiest path to victory is managing to mint an access token for any user, a task made way easier by the "cursed" JavaScript bundle they found at an endpoint containing hard-coded administrator credentials. These were likely meant for the staging environment, but the duo estimated, correctly, that they could be leveraged nevertheless.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

At this point, they ran into the WAF in front of the service. A Web Application Firewall is similar to a network firewall, but instead of working with IPs and ports, it considers endpoints (URLs) and the requirements to access them. The researchers hypothesize that although it's a good and standard practice, the WAF was put in place because of how bad things were underneath.

And they were right. The app decompilation had revealed a "pinService", and Shah found that it was accessible through the WAF. From thereon, they found "getUser", and correctly guessed that they could retrieve users' information with their email, phone, and ID. Remember those admin credentials? They came in handy, revealing the users' password hashes, but as these were SHA-512, cracking them was unfeasible.

At this point, they let GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra loose to brute-force path names, and found an unprotected one that ultimately let them overwrite any user's password, partially enabling taking over their accounts. However, there was still MFA to contend with.

As it turns out, even that too was misconfigured, as the Australian environment would let users skip MFA entirely. With some judicious token shuffling across endpoints and the mobile app, they eventually could mint access tokens, letting them fully impersonate any user account... and unlock their cars. Then, it was as simple as sending out an API request for the "door-unlock" command, and sure enough, the test car promptly opened.

#10191. Introducing Falcon-H1-Arabic: Pushing the Boundaries of Arabic Language AI with Hybrid Architecture

Discover more in our official blogpost, featuring an interactive experience

The journey of building world-class Arabic language models has been one of continuous learning and iteration. Today, we're excited to announce Falcon-H1-Arabic, our most advanced Arabic language model family to date, representing a significant leap forward in both architecture and capabilities. This release embodies months of research, community feedback, and technical innovation, culminating in three powerful models that set new standards for Arabic natural language processing.

When we launched Falcon-Arabic a few months ago, the response from the community was both humbling and enlightening. Developers, researchers and students across the Arab world used the model for real use cases, pushing them to its limits and providing invaluable feedback. We learned where the model excelled and, more importantly, where it struggled. Long-context understanding, dialectal variations, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific knowledge emerged as key areas requiring deeper attention.

We didn't just want to make incremental improvements, we wanted to fundamentally rethink our approach. The result is Falcon-H1-Arabic, a model family that addresses every piece of feedback we received while introducing architectural innovations that were previously unexplored in Arabic language modeling.

Falcon-H1-Arabic 3B, 7B, 34B models outperforming all SOTA models of similar sizes and sometimes bigger.

Falcon-H1-Arabic is built on the Falcon-H1 hybrid architecture, which integrates State Space Models (Mamba) and Transformer attention within every block. Both components run in parallel and their representations are fused before the block’s output projection. This design provides the linear-time scalability of Mamba for extremely long sequences while preserving the precise long-range modeling capabilities of attention. For Arabic, with its rich morphology and flexible sentence structures, this approach significantly improves coherence and reasoning across extended text. We've deployed this architecture across three scales (3B, 7B, 34B parameters), each balancing capacity, efficiency, and deployability for different use cases from edge devices to enterprise applications.

Falcon-H1 architecture. Attention and SSM run in parallel within each block; their outputs are concatenated before the block’s output projection. The number of SSM/Attention heads depends on the model size. More details on the Falcon-H1 technical report.

We've dramatically increased context capabilities from Falcon-Arabic's 32K limit to 128K tokens for the 3B model and 256K tokens for both the 7B and 34B models. At 256K tokens (~200,000 words), these models can process several novels or hundreds of pages of technical documentation enabling applications in legal analysis, medical records, academic research, and extended conversations that were previously impractical. Our post-training specifically addresses "lost in the middle" challenges to ensure models effectively utilize their full context range, not just accept long inputs.

We rebuilt our pre-training data pipeline from the ground up to better reflect the complexity of Arabic. This began with a multi-stage quality filtering process tailored to Arabic orthography, morphology, diacritics, and syntactic patterns. Instead of heuristic filtering, we used deep linguistic analysis to isolate coherent, well-structured text and remove noise commonly found in open-web corpora. The result is a significantly cleaner, more stylistically consistent Arabic dataset.

Dialect coverage was another key priority. Arabic is not monolithic; Modern Standard Arabic coexists with dialects such as Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, and Maghrebi, each with distinct vocabularies and grammatical constructions. We expanded dialectal sources substantially so the models would understand and generate the full spectrum of real-world Arabic rather than leaning disproportionately toward formal MSA. To maintain global reasoning and domain diversity, we also preserved the multilingual capabilities of Falcon-H1 by training the Arabic models on an almost equal mix of Arabic, English, and multilingual content totalling around 300 Billion Tokens. This ensures strong performance in code, STEM, and cross-lingual reasoning. The following figure illustrates the distribution of the pre-training data across languages and categories. All values are expressed in billions of tokens.

After pre-training, Falcon-H1-Arabic undergoes a focused post-training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). During SFT, we expose the models to high-quality Arabic instructions, curated long-context examples, and structured reasoning tasks that teach them to follow directives, maintain coherence over extended sequences, and ground their responses in relevant information. This stage is crucial for ensuring that the models can actually use their large context windows which does not emerge automatically from architecture alone.

We follow SFT with a targeted DPO phase to refine alignment, conversational quality, and preference consistency. DPO helps the models balance long-context reasoning with general linguistic competence, improving helpfulness and reducing common failure modes such as drifting, overuse of context, or neglecting earlier information. Throughout both stages, we carefully monitor for catastrophic forgetting and maintain a controlled curriculum so gains in long-context behavior do not come at the expense of core reasoning or factual accuracy. The result is a family of models that handles extended documents and dialogue with ease while preserving strong performance on everyday language tasks.

Beyond benchmark-oriented optimization, our post-training process deliberately strengthens areas that traditional evaluations do not fully capture, including conversational faithfulness, rhetorical organization, structured follow-ups, and discourse coherence. These enhancements significantly boost the model’s practical usefulness, making Falcon-H1-Arabic more dependable in real multi-turn dialogue, instruction execution, and long-context conversational flows.

Numbers tell an important part of the story. On the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard (OALL), a comprehensive benchmark evaluating Arabic language understanding across diverse tasks, Falcon-H1-Arabic achieves state-of-the-art results at every scale we tested. Note that our scores may vary slightly from those reported on the leaderboard, as we used vLLM as the backend instead of the leaderboard’s Accelerate-based implementation. These differences are typically under one point while offering significantly faster runtime.

Beyond OALL, we also report results on the 3LM benchmark for STEM-related tasks on both synthetic and native splits; Arabculture for Arabic culture assessment; and AraDice for Arabic dialect coverage across Levantine, and Egyptian varieties as well as Arabic culture across 6 countries. The reported AraDice score is the average of all the 3 scores.

Starting with the 3B model, the performance is exceptional. It reaches approximately 62% on OALL, outperforming all small-scale models, including Gemma-4B, Qwen3-4B, and Phi-4-mini by roughly ten points. On 3LM, the main Arabic STEM benchmark, it scores around 82% on the native split and 73% on the synthetic split. It also achieves about 62% on the ArabCulture benchmark and around 50% across AraDice dialect evaluation (Egyptian, Gulf, and Levantine). This makes Falcon-H1-Arabic-3B a high-quality, highly efficient model suitable for edge deployments, real-time applications, and agentic systems where latency and cost matter.

The 7B model continues this upward trajectory. With a score of 71.7% on OALL, it surpasses all models in the ~10B class, including Fanar-9B, Allam-7B*, and Qwen3-8B. On 3LM, it reaches about 92% on the native split and 85% on the synthetic one. AraDice scores rise into the mid-50s across all dialects, and ArabCulture results approach 80%. This model strikes an ideal balance between capability and deployability, making it the most practical choice for general-purpose Arabic NLP in production environments.

The 34B model represents our flagship system and establishes a new state of the art for Arabic language modeling. It reaches approximately 75% on OALL, outperforming not only models of similar size but even much larger systems such as Llama-3.3-70B and AceGPT2-32B. Its 3LM scores reach about 96% on the native split and 94% on the synthetic one. On ArabCulture it scores close to 80%, and on AraDice it reaches around 53 across dialects. The fact that a 34B hybrid model surpasses the performance of 70B-scale transformers demonstrates the effectiveness of the Falcon-H1 architecture, the quality of the data, and the strength of the post-training pipeline.

These benchmark results validate our approach but also highlight an important reality: the frontier of Arabic language modeling is advancing rapidly. Each percentage point on these benchmarks represents countless hours of engineering effort, careful dataset curation, and architectural refinement. The margins by which Falcon-H1-Arabic leads aren't just statistical artifacts, they translate to meaningfully better user experiences in real-world applications.

Each model in the Falcon-H1-Arabic family is suited to different deployment scenarios. The 3B model is optimized for speed, cost-efficiency, and high-throughput systems, making it ideal for agentic workflows, on-device applications, low-latency chat, and environments with strict resource constraints. The 7B model serves as the general-purpose workhorse for most production applications, powering document understanding systems, chatbots, summarization pipelines, and content generation tools. The 34B model is designed for high-stakes domains where accuracy and long-range reasoning matter most, including legal analysis, medical summarization, academic research, and large-scale enterprise automation. Its extended context window makes it uniquely capable of analyzing hundreds of pages of text in a single pass while maintaining precise coherence.

Like all language models, Falcon-H1-Arabic may reflect biases from training data and can produce hallucinated information. Model outputs should not be used as sole authorities for medical, legal, or financial decisions without professional verification. Long-context performance may degrade at extreme ranges. We recommend task-specific evaluation and appropriate guardrails before deployment in production or sensitive applications.

This work stands on the shoulders of many. We extend our gratitude to the Arabic NLP research community, whose open sharing of benchmarks, datasets, and methodologies enables progress across the field. Special thanks to our colleagues at TII: Ilyas Chahed, Younes Belkada, Dhia Eddine Rhaiem, Puneesh Khanna, Jingwei Zuo, Mikhail Lubinets, Slim Frikha, Maksim Velikanov, Kacper Piskorski, and Suhail Mohmad for their invaluable support during this project.

Impressive milestone for Arabic language AI. Falcon-H1-Arabic’s hybrid architecture is a strong step toward closing the performance gap in high-quality Arabic understanding and generation. Exciting to see innovation that’s not just scaling models, but rethinking architecture to better capture the richness and complexity of Arabic. #10190. Hunter is killing Google Home, Alexa controls for its smart ceiling fans

Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.

Effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls. Hunter’s app and the included remote will continue to work, but connections to smart home ecosystems will not.

Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.

After this date, Google home and Alexa functionality that relies on this legacy cloud connection will no longer work for HunterSMART fans, including voice commands, scenes, and automations.

This bridge is going away in favor of a Matter connection, with Hunter having been upgrading select models to be Matter-compatible over the past year. But this is only available to “eligible” models, not everyone who was already using Hunter’s existing bridge. A list of compatible models is available on Hunter’s website, with firmware updates rolling out via the HunterSMART app.

Some models, such as the one I reviewed a few years ago, require updated hardware. Besides that, the one I have can’t even be re-connected to Wi-Fi to check for an update as Hunter’s Android app consistently crashes during the setup process.

Once the fan has been updated, it won’t be available via the existing link and will instead require re-pairing via your smart home app of choice, whether that’s Google Home or another.

…Hunter is transitioning eligible HunterSMART™ products to Matter, an industry standard designed to support broader smart-home compatibility.

If your fan is eligible for Matter-compatibility, you will be able to continue using all smart functionality within the Google Home and/or Alexa ecosystems after completing the applicable Matter migration & setup.

Once your HunterSMART fan is Matter-enabled, connecting your fan to Google and Alexa will work differently than it does today. Instead of linking your HunterSMART account to Google Home or Alexa, you will need to setup your Matter-enabled fan directly into these compatible ecosystems using the Matter setup available via the Google Home and/or Alexa apps. Matter-enabled devices do not use the legacy cloud linking service for smart controls that is being discontinued.

How can I migrate my HunterSMART fan to Matter?

Depending on your fan model and hardware configuration, a firmware update or updated hardware components may be required for Matter compatibility. Available Matter upgrade options and instructions will vary by product. You can visit our HunterSMART™ Matter resource page for the latest information about Matter compatibility, available upgrade options, and next steps.
