#10189. How ‘Boring’ Businesses Can Turn Black Friday Into a Competitive Advantage

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. Here’s how small businesses can attract customers, boost sales and stand out without big budgets.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. It’s also an opportunity for the hardworking small businesses we see every day, from bakeries and hair salons to cleaning companies and accounting firms.

I affectionately call them “boring” businesses, but there’s nothing boring about the people behind them. They’re the familiar neighborhood businesses we rely on every day, run by hardworking people who often wear several hats to keep things going.

And these traditional industries continue to attract new entrepreneurs. According to internal Tailor Brands business formation data, cleaning and home service businesses saw growth ranging from 60% to more than 300% in 2026, depending on the subcategory. But whether you’re just starting out or have been serving your community for years, the challenge is the same: finding ways to attract customers and keep them coming back.

Black Friday gives small businesses an opportunity to do both. A record 202.9 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday in 2025, up from 197 million in 2024, as reported by inBeat. While much of the attention goes to major retailers, local businesses can use the shopping season to reconnect with existing customers and give new ones a reason to try their services.

Having worked with many small businesses, I’ve learned that successful Black Friday campaigns don’t always require big budgets or massive discounts. Sometimes, a personal gesture or a clever offer can make all the difference.

Here are a few practical strategies, including examples from my own experience, to help everyday businesses make the most of Black Friday.

Whether you run a hair salon, accounting firm or neighborhood bakery, Black Friday can be an opportunity to generate sales from customers who already know and trust your business. Instead of competing for attention with another promotional email, try sending a handwritten offer.

Handwrytten’s Consumer Survey found that only 11% of consumers had recently received a handwritten note from a brand, and just 4% found them annoying. That makes handwritten outreach an interesting way to stand out during a season dominated by digital promotions.

I’ve seen this work firsthand. I once worked with a client whose cake business was on the verge of bankruptcy. With bills and taxes piling up, we asked the owner’s 10-year-old daughter to handwrite thank-you letters to existing customers, offering them a special Black Friday deal: buy cake credits now and redeem them anytime over the next 12 months.

We sold credits for 271 cakes at an average of almost €60 each, generating nearly €16,000 in Black Friday sales. That cash injection gave the business much-needed breathing room. Customers also loved the letters, and the heartwarming gesture helped turn them into even more loyal supporters.

The same idea can work for almost any local business. Hair salons can sell prepaid appointments, cleaning companies can offer service credits, and accountants can create annual packages. The trick is to combine a personal touch with an offer that brings in revenue today while giving customers something valuable tomorrow.

For hotels, Black Friday is an opportunity to sell discounted spa weekends, romantic getaways and prepaid stays during the quieter winter months. But travelers need to discover these offers before they can book them.

AI-powered travel planning creates another opportunity to reach potential guests. According to Wanderboat, 56% of active U.S. travelers used AI for some aspect of their travel experience in the previous year.

Yet ranking highly on Google doesn’t guarantee visibility in AI-generated answers. Heroic Rankings reports that Google’s AI overlooks approximately 62% of pages ranking in the top 10 traditional search results.

To improve their chances of appearing in AI-generated recommendations, hotels should make their Black Friday offers as specific as possible. Instead of simply advertising “40% off winter stays,” imagine a small hotel offering a “Two-night spa getaway for two in Asheville for $299, including breakfast and spa access, valid December 12–14.”

I’d create a dedicated page for that offer, clearly listing the price, dates, amenities, cancellation policy and booking conditions. I’d also add guest reviews and answer questions travelers might ask, such as whether parking is included or if the spa requires advance booking. Make sure the details match what’s listed on booking platforms and add appropriate structured data to help search engines understand the package.

The easier it is for AI to find and understand your offer, the better your chances of reaching travelers looking for exactly that kind of getaway.

But optimizing your own website is only part of the equation. I’d also try to get my Black Friday offer featured in local media, relevant industry websites and articles rounding up the best Black Friday deals. In its GEO research, CSP analyzed more than 70,000 AI answers across three industries in 2026 and found that 85 earned-media placements generated 5,697 AI citations. This shows why getting your offer mentioned on relevant third-party websites can be just as important as making it easy to find on your own.

Video can make even the most ordinary services more appealing. In fact, 85% of consumers say they’ve been convinced to buy a product or service after watching a video, as reported by Flova. Even less flashy businesses like accounting firms, plumbers and cleaning companies can use humor to make their Black Friday campaigns stand out.

Last year, while managing a marketing campaign for a cleaning company, I wanted to create a funny video, but the employees weren’t comfortable on camera. We used AI animation instead, creating a humorous clip about the mess after a holiday party. The video converted particularly well in paid campaigns, driving plenty of sales while also generating strong organic engagement.

What makes this approach even more attractive today is how affordable it has become to experiment. As GPTProto reports, short AI video clips can cost between $0.04 and $0.50 per generation. That doesn’t mean producing an entire campaign costs a few cents, but it does mean small businesses can test different concepts, jokes and visual styles without spending heavily on every attempt.

I’ve since started incorporating AI video into the marketing services I offer clients. For a small business with someone comfortable using AI tools, the opportunity isn’t simply to produce cheaper videos. It’s to experiment with more ideas, discover what resonates with customers and put the strongest creative into a Black Friday campaign.

Small businesses can try the same approach. Show a relatable problem, add some humor, and finish with a clear Black Friday offer. You don’t need a big budget to make an ordinary service memorable.

Organic search traffic is declining across many industries, partly because Google’s AI Overviews now answer informational queries directly. According to Get Stuff Digital, organic traffic declined by 20% to 35% in its analysis following the introduction of AI-powered search features.

But I don’t see this as a reason to panic. Small businesses don’t necessarily need more informational traffic. They need visitors who are ready to book or buy. That’s why I’d focus Black Friday SEO efforts on high-intent searches rather than trying to recover every lost click.

For example, a cleaning company could create a dedicated page targeting searches like “Black Friday cleaning deals in Chicago” or “holiday deep cleaning discounts in Chicago,” with a specific package, price and clear booking option. I’d publish that page in September, or early October at the latest, to give Google time to discover and index it before Black Friday. I’d also add a few relevant internal links from existing service pages and blog posts to help search engines find it.

The goal isn’t to attract the most traffic. It’s to make sure that when someone searches for a Black Friday deal on a service you provide, your business is there with an offer they can act on.

Black Friday isn’t just about attracting new customers. It’s also a chance to bring back shoppers who never completed their purchases.

The average cart abandonment rate is 70.22%, as reported by Knowcrunch. These shoppers have already shown interest, making them a valuable audience for Black Friday offers.

For my clients, I already use automated emails year-round to remind customers about products they’ve left in their carts. During Black Friday, I take this a step further by targeting shoppers who abandoned their carts in the past 30 to 60 days and sending them personalized emails with a limited-time discount.

AI agents can make this process even easier by helping generate messages based on the products each customer considered. Scalably reports that sales professionals expect AI agents to reduce email-drafting time by 36% once fully implemented. In my experience, automating these repetitive follow-ups can save even more time, especially when you’re managing campaigns for multiple clients.

For example, a furniture store could automatically email someone who abandoned a sofa in their cart, remind them of the exact product and offer a Black Friday discount with a direct link to checkout. The system should also exclude customers who’ve already completed their purchases, so they don’t receive unnecessary reminders.

Instead of spending your entire Black Friday budget attracting new visitors, use automated emails and timely discounts to bring interested shoppers back and turn abandoned carts into sales.

One of the first rules of marketing is to be where your customers are. And sometimes, that’s behind the wheel. Munley Law highlights that Americans spend an average of 60.2 minutes driving each day. For local businesses, that creates an opportunity to reach customers during the busy Black Friday weekend.

Run short, frequent local radio ads with one clear offer and a promo code. Leave flyers with a time-limited deal on parked cars in busy shopping areas, where local rules allow.

Extend your opening hours over the holiday weekend and add them as special hours in your Google Business Profile. Drivers searching “near me” early in the morning or late in the evening may be looking for businesses they can visit immediately, so longer hours give you more opportunities to attract them. Add your offers to the profile too, and if your business allows it, offer curbside pickup.

Plan for parking, too. Reserve a few spots near the entrance for pickups. If you need more, offer to rent a few spaces from a neighbor just for the holiday weekend. Many will say no, but a small business only needs a handful of spots, and some neighbors will gladly take a few extra dollars for them. Then tell customers where to park in your emails and Google Business Profile.

On Cyber Monday, extend the deal online for anyone who heard the ad but didn’t make it in.

Giving away a small service can be a smart Black Friday strategy when it helps customers take the first step toward a much larger purchase. A limited-time offer gives them a reason to act now rather than keep postponing their decision.

Dental practices are a good example. According to Myra, 23% of adults have delayed dental treatment because of its cost. Offering a free initial consultation during Black Friday can remove that first financial barrier and encourage patients to explore treatments they might otherwise put off.

For example, a dental practice could invite patients considering implants, veneers or orthodontic treatment to book a complimentary examination and personalized treatment plan, with clinically appropriate imaging where needed. The dentist can explain the options, discuss installment payments if available and help patients understand the costs before committing.

And it’s not always just about money. Some patients feel anxious about visiting the dentist or discovering they need extensive treatment. A free, no-obligation first appointment can make that step feel less intimidating while giving the practice an opportunity to build trust.

The appointment can take place after Black Friday, as long as it’s booked during the promotion. For treatments involving a significant financial commitment, even a few new patients could make the offer worthwhile.

If there’s one thing I’ve learned from working with small businesses, it’s that a successful Black Friday campaign doesn’t have to be complicated or expensive. Sometimes, understanding your customers and coming up with a creative offer is enough to stand out.

My advice is to pick one or two strategies that make sense for your business, test them, and learn from the results. You might be surprised by what works.

Black Friday isn’t just for big retailers. It’s also an opportunity for the hardworking small businesses we see every day, from bakeries and hair salons to cleaning companies and accounting firms.

I affectionately call them “boring” businesses, but there’s nothing boring about the people behind them. They’re the familiar neighborhood businesses we rely on every day, run by hardworking people who often wear several hats to keep things going.

And these traditional industries continue to attract new entrepreneurs. According to internal Tailor Brands business formation data, cleaning and home service businesses saw growth ranging from 60% to more than 300% in 2026, depending on the subcategory. But whether you’re just starting out or have been serving your community for years, the challenge is the same: finding ways to attract customers and keep them coming back.

#10188. Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

“BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

The other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”

Technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

#10187. NVIDIA Cosmos Reason 2 Brings Advanced Reasoning To Physical AI

NVIDIA today released Cosmos Reason 2, the latest advancement in open, reasoning vision language models for physical AI. Cosmos Reason 2 surpasses its previous version in accuracy and tops the Physical AI Bench and Physical Reasoning leaderboards as the #1 open model for visual understanding.

Since their introduction, vision-language models have rapidly improved at tasks like object and pattern recognition in images. But they still struggle with tasks humans find natural, like planning several steps ahead, dealing with uncertainty or adapting to new situations. Cosmos Reason is designed to close this gap by giving robots and AI agents stronger common sense and reasoning to solve complex problems step by step.

Cosmos Reason 2 is a state-of-the-art, open reasoning vision-language model (VLM) that enables robots and AI agents to see, understand, plan, and act in the physical world like humans. It uses common sense, physics, and prior knowledge to recognize how objects move across space and time to handle complex tasks, adapt to new situations, and figure out how to solve problems step by step.

Improved spatio-temporal understanding and timestamp precision.

Optimized performance with flexible deployment options from edge to cloud with 2B and 8B parameters model sizes.

Support for expanded set of spatial understanding and visual perception capabilities — 2D/3D point localization, bounding box coordinates, trajectory data, and OCR support.

Improved long-context understanding with 256K input tokens, up from 16K with Cosmos Reason 1.

Adaptable to multiple use cases with easy-to-use Cosmos Cookbook recipes.

Video analytics AI agents — These agents can extract valuable insights from massive volumes of video data to optimize processes. Cosmos Reason 2 builds on the capabilities of Cosmos Reason 1 and now provides OCR support, as well as 2D/3D point localization and a set of mark understanding.

Developers can jumpstart development of video analytics AI agents by using the NVIDIA blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Salesforce is transforming workplace safety and compliance by analyzing video footage captured by Cobalt robots with Agentforce and VSS blueprint with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Data annotation and critique — Enable developers to automate high-quality annotation and critique of massive, diverse training datasets. Cosmos Reason provides time stamps and detailed descriptions for real or synthetically generated training videos.

Uber is exploring Cosmos Reason 2 to deliver accurate, searchable video captions for autonomous vehicle (AV) training data, enabling efficient identification of critical driving scenarios. This co-authored Reason 2 for AV Video Captioning and VQA recipe demonstrates how to fine-tune and evaluate Cosmos Reason 2-8B on annotated AV videos. Across multiple evaluation metrics, measurable improvements were achieved: BLEU scores improved 10.6% (0.113 → 0.125), MCQ-based VQA gained 0.67 percentage points (80.18% → 80.85%), and LingoQA increased 13.8% (63.2% → 77.0%). These gains demonstrate effective domain adaptation for AV applications.

Robot planning and reasoning — Act as the brain for deliberate, methodical decision-making in a robot vision language action (VLA) model. Cosmos Reason 2 now provides trajectory coordinates in addition to determining next steps.

Encord provides native support for Cosmos Reason 2 in its Data Agent library and AI data platform, enabling developers to leverage Cosmos Reason 2 as a VLA for robotics and other physical AI use cases.

Companies like Hitachi, Milestone and VAST Data are using Cosmos Reason to advance robotics, autonomous driving, and video analytics AI agents for traffic and workplace safety.

Try Cosmos Reason 2 on build.nvidia.com and experience the latest features with sample prompts for generating bounding boxes and robot trajectories. Upload your own videos and images for further analysis.

Download Cosmos Reason 2 models (2B and 8B) on Hugging Face or use Cosmos Reason 2 in the cloud. The model will be available soon on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. To get started, check out Cosmos Reason 2 documentation and the Cosmos Cookbook.

Cosmos Predict is a generative AI model that predicts future states of the physical world as video, based on text, image, or video inputs.

Cosmos Transfer is our lightest multicontrol model built for video to world style transfer.

NVIDIA GR00T N1.6 is an open reasoning vision language action (VLA) model, purpose-built for humanoid robots, that unlocks full body control and uses NVIDIA Cosmos Reason for better reasoning and contextual understanding.

#10186. This Billionaire Invested in OpenAI in 2019. Here’s What He’s Betting on Next.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This billionaire is betting that AI will revamp websites as we know them.

He made billions betting on what’s next. Now this 71-year-old investor’s latest move reflects his conviction that AI will change how the Internet works.

Vinod Khosla’s venture capital firm, Khosla Ventures, made early investments in OpenAI, DoorDash and Instacart. His latest investment, AI startup Coframe, targets another potential shift: how websites operate. Coframe wants to rewire the Internet so every visitor to a website sees a page custom-made for them.

“The world has changed because AI has enabled extreme customization,” Khosla said in an interview with Business Insider. Forbes reported earlier this year that Khosla’s net worth is around $10 billion.

Coframe announced this week that it raised $35 million in total funding, including a $25 million Series A led by Khosla Ventures and Hanabi Capital. Executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind also participated.

Coframe helps businesses improve their websites so more people buy something, sign up for something or take another desired action. The startup creates and tests different versions of a webpage, including text, images and design. It then tracks how visitors interact with the webpage to determine how to improve it.

For example, say an online store wants to sell more shoes. Coframe could help the company test different headlines, product images or page layouts and determine which versions lead to more purchases.

“For decades, the web has been frozen in place, showing every visitor essentially the same page,” Khosla said in the press release. “Coframe is building the living internet, where two people can visit the same website and have completely different experiences, personalized to who they are and what they need. These interfaces continuously learn and improve themselves. This is a huge leap beyond traditional A/B testing and the next iteration of the internet.”

Coframe claims that it can help businesses get more out of the visitors they already have and spend far less time figuring out how to capitalize on their audiences. The startup said in the press release that its AI-powered testing platform has helped customers generate more than $300 million in additional revenue, with conversion rates improving by more than 20% on average.

Coframe’s customers include Dropbox, BCG, Block, Backcountry and Sur La Table.

Speed is another part of the startup’s appeal. Coframe said it built and launched an experiment for Dropbox in 30 minutes that previously would have required four weeks of engineering, design and quality-assurance work. For an unnamed Fortune 500 customer, the company said it launched dozens of variations and increased conversions by 70% within 30 days of the contract being signed.

The idea is to let businesses try more approaches without adding weeks of production work each time. Faster testing can help teams identify promising changes and move past unsuccessful ones sooner.

Khosla sees AI as a way to deliver an experience built around each visitor to a website, like Coframe is doing.

“The alternative is to write code for every page that’s presented, but that’s too expensive and way too slow,” Khosla told Business Insider. “This idea of a customized page for every user is a really good idea.”

#10185. A Practical Introduction to the Twitch Helix API

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Behind almost every Twitch tool you have ever seen, the stat trackers, the moderation bots, the stream overlays, the alert systems, sits one interface: the Twitch Helix API. Twitch is unusually generous with public data, and Helix is the door to it. If you have ever wondered how third-party sites know who is live, what a channel's viewership looks like, or details a Twitch profile page does not even display, this is the machinery.

This article is a practical overview of Helix for developers who have not used it yet: what it offers, how its authentication works, what people build with it, and where the sharp edges are.

Helix is Twitch's current REST API, served from api.twitch.tv/helix. It replaced the old "Kraken" API, which was fully retired in 2022, so any tutorial still showing Kraken endpoints is a sign to keep scrolling. Helix covers users, streams, channels, games and categories, clips, chat, moderation actions, subscriptions, and events, with JSON in and JSON out.

Two things distinguish it from many platform APIs. First, a large share of it works without any user's permission, because the data is public by Twitch's own definition. Second, it is paired with EventSub, a push system that notifies your application when things happen (a stream goes live, a user follows, a message arrives) instead of forcing you to poll. Most serious Twitch tools use both: Helix for lookups, EventSub for live events.

Authentication is where most newcomers stall, mainly because Twitch offers several OAuth flows and tutorials rarely say which one you actually need. The short version:

Every request needs a Client ID, which you get by registering an application in the Twitch developer console (two-factor authentication on your account is required first). Requests carry the Client ID and a bearer token together; forgetting the Client ID header is the classic mystery 401.

App access tokens come from the client credentials flow, a single server-to-server request with your ID and secret. They have no user attached and that is fine, because public reads, user profiles, live streams, top games, clips, need no user context. For most read-only tools, this is the only flow you ever touch.

Tokens expire, so real applications cache them with their reported lifetime and refresh on a 401 rather than assuming a token lives forever.

A tour of the endpoints that power most tools:

Users. Give the users endpoint a username and it returns the account's public record: display name, profile image, description, Affiliate or Partner status, and the account's exact creation timestamp. That last field is interesting because Twitch does not display it anywhere on a profile, yet it is one of the platform's most useful trust signals, moderators use account age to spot throwaway accounts, and streamers use it to filter giveaway entries. The creation date alone powers a small subcategory of tools: free account age checkers, such as Twitch account age checker, are essentially this one endpoint with a clean page around it, taking any public username and returning the creation date, age, avatar, and broadcaster status. It is a good illustration of how far a single well-chosen Helix field can go.

Streams. The stream's endpoint reports who is live right now, with titles, categories, thumbnail URLs, and viewer counts. This is the backbone of every "is my favorite streamer live" notifier and every directory-style site, and polling it over time is how stat trackers chart viewership history.

Games and categories. Top games, category search, and metadata. Combined with streams data, this is how analytics sites rank categories and how tools answer "how crowded is this category right now."

Clips and videos. Clip metadata, view counts, and creation tools. Highlight compilers and clip-sharing bots live here.

Helix enforces a points-based rate limit per Client ID, and every response tells you where you stand through Ratelimit-Limit, Ratelimit-Remaining, and Ratelimit-Reset headers. Well-behaved tools read those headers and back off before hitting zero; badly behaved ones retry 429s in a loop and wonder why things get worse. For lookup-style tools the practical fix is caching, data like account creation dates never changes, so there is no reason to ask twice.

A few more edges worth knowing before they bite:

Usernames change, IDs do not. Store user IDs, not logins, or your saved data will eventually point at the wrong person.

Missing users are not errors. Looking up a nonexistent username returns a successful response with an empty data array, so handle the empty case explicitly.

Batching exists. The users endpoint takes up to 100 logins in one call, which matters the moment your tool checks lists instead of individuals.

Secrets stay server-side. The client secret identifies your application; calling the token endpoint from browser code hands your app's identity to anyone who opens devtools. Public-facing tools put a small server between the browser and Twitch.

The reason Twitch's third-party ecosystem is so large is that the barrier is so low: one public API, generous free access, and a platform where small questions genuinely matter to people. That is why the space is full of narrow tools that each answer one thing well, when was this account created, is this channel live, how fast is this category growing, which clips popped this week. Most of them are a weekend of work on top of one or two endpoints, and some of them grow into real products.

If you want to start, the path is short: register an application at the developer console, request an app access token, and call the users or streams endpoint for something you actually care about. The official documentation at dev.twitch.tv is current and well maintained, which is not something every platform can claim. Pick one piece of data Twitch collects but does not display, put a clean interface on it, and you are following the same recipe as most of the Twitch tools you already use.

Seagate wants you to side-load an SSD in its latest external hard drive.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's old is new again. Seagate started adding faster flash-based storage to its hard drives in 2010, when solid-state storage was prohibitively expensive. And now that SSDs are stupid-expensive again (thanks, AI hyperscaler demand) the hard drive maker is offering up another hybrid drive, of sorts, with the Firecuda Forge.

Available in 8TB and 20TB capacities, the Forge is an external hard drive that requires that you bring and install your own SSD. That's right, the drive won't work unless you partially disassemble and install your own M.2 2280 SSD, which mounts in the side of the enclosure. 1TB drives with DRAM are recommended. Performance maxes out at PCIe Gen3 drives; newer, faster, and roomier SSDs are supported, but won't improve performance. The Firecuda Forge only has a mounting point for 2280-length drives, and while drives that are less than 1TB are supported, that means less room for frequently used files, so "performance may be reduced."

Interestingly, Seagate sent us a 2TB FireCuda 530R SSD to test with the Forge hard drive, which is both faster (PCIe 4.0) and more spacious than what the company says you should pair with its hard drive. The list of SSD that Seagate has officially qualified to work with the Firecuda Forge is also pretty sparse, including just three other drives: Samsung's 990 Pro, WD/Sandisk SN850X/GX Pro 850X, and the WD/SanDisk SN710/GX7100.

We only received a review sample a few days before launch, and haven't yet had a chance to put the FireCuda Forge through its paces for a full review. But I was impressed that, after I installed the SSD and plugged the drive in, it just showed up in Windows 11 as an 8TB drive. (The company says it also works with macOS 26 and later). There was no software setup involved, and Seagate says you can even remove and upgrade the hard drive to something roomier down the line. Seagate calls the "product architecture" that handles unifying and data handling between the spinning platter drive and the SSD "Alkemi," and says it combines "onboard processing" with the hard drive and the user-supplied SSD to "prioritize active data without requiring users to manually manage separate drives."

Seagate says Alkemi observes workloads and gives priority to currently relevant or often-used data, that it adapts over time to user behavior, and describes it as an "on-device device dynamic caching and workload-aware data-prioritization technology." That sounds pretty similar to the SSD caching used on hybrid drives of the early 2010s, although with up to 1TB of fast SSD storage, you're getting a much bigger fast data pool than those drives of the past, which often made do with 4-16GB.

Interestingly, Seagate says that machine learning is a part of what Alkemi does, but repeatedly points out in its review materials that it is not using generative AI. It's likely the company is worried about customers connecting the many reported instances of LLMs and agents deleting data with this new product. I can understand why Seagate would want to distance its hybrid storage tech from reports of catastrophic data deletion.

Getting past the somewhat odd-feeling aspect of having to crack open an external drive right out of the box and install another drive into it in order for it to work, the process was pretty painless. You have to remove four screws from the bottom (with a tiny included hex-bit driver) to get the outer shell off the FireCuda Forge. From there, the M.2 drive bay is clearly visible on the side. If you want to remove six more hex screws, you can also pop out the hard drive for future upgrades. But for now, we're just going to install an M.2 SSD.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

SSD installation is pretty much the same as putting one of these drives in any laptop or motherboard. Though you'll need a tool; the drive requires a a tiny screw and Seagate does not include a suitable Phillips head screwdriver. The drive bay is somewhat recessed, and there are two thick thermal pads included in the box that should ensure the drive makes contact with both the inner edge of the bay and the external shroud.

This should provide some heat dissipation, but these surfaces are all's plastic, with only a foil layer on the outer shroud to draw some of the drive's heat away from the SSD itself. This is probably fine for most bursty game and creative workloads. But this design does not feel ideal for workloads that hit the drive consistently for hours on end. During our testing, the edge of the drive where the SSD is installed got noticeably warmer than the rest of the enclosure, but it didn't get hot.

In terms of design, the FireCuda Forge looks very similar to the FireCuda X Vault HDD we looked at earlier this year, complete with some gamer-friendly RGB lighting. The primary physical difference is that you'll need the supplied USB-C cable and external power adapter to use the Forge, while the X Vault only has a USB-C port. Presumably, powering both a 3.5-inch hard drive and an M.2 SSD draws too much power for most (or at least some) USB-C ports. I still would love for drives like this to be able to run off of one single cable, though, which was my favorite feature of the X Vault hard drive.

We only received the FireCuda Forge a couple of working days before its announcement. But we were able to run some benchmarks with the Forge drive and a 530R SSD that Seagate provided, and saw some interesting results. The Forge's USB-C connection is USB4, and Seagate's performance claims are up to 2,500 MB/s read and 2,000 MB/s write. That's obviously much faster than a hard drive, but you're also going to be sacrificing the speed of the SSD you're dropping into this drive — especially if it's a PCIe 4.0 SSD.

PCMark 10 is a trace-based benchmark that uses a wide-ranging set of real-world traces from popular applications and everyday tasks to measure the performance of storage devices.

On this synthetic test, Seagate's Forge beats recent traditional hard drives (and the slowest external SSD we've tested, Samsung's T5). But Kingston's fast flash drive does better, as does Sandisk's Desk Drive, which nearly doubles the score of the Forge, which isn't surprising given it's a full-fledged external SSD.

We use the DiskBench storage benchmarking tool to test file transfer performance with a custom 50GB dataset. We copy 4,617 files (images, videos, and software ISO files) to a folder on the test drive (write). Then, after leaving the system idle for five minutes, we run the same test in reverse, moving the test folder to a different location on our PCIe 4.0 testing drive.

Here , we see the Forge drive easily beating the spinning-platter-only drives and Samsung's T5 Evo on writes, only falling to the SanDisk Desk Drive desktop SSD. But on reads, the Forge leads by the pack.

CrystalDiskMark (CDM) is a free and easy-to-run storage benchmarking tool that SSD companies commonly use to assign performance specifications to their products. It gives us insight into how each device handles different file sizes. We run this test at its default settings.

Last up (for now), CrystalDiskMark proves the Forge does benefit significantly from its USB4 interface, with its performance on sequential reads and writes jumping well ahead of everything else on our chart — because all other drives here top out at 10 Gbps. There are, of course, faster external SSDs (like Samsung's recent P9). But at 8TB, solid-state options are generally more expensive, and faster external SSDs at 8TB are much more expensive. And of course, 20TB external SSDs aren't really an option, at least in the consumer drive space.

The whole reason a product like the Seagate Forge exists is because SSDs are expensive. The problem is, hard drives have faced similar price jumps due to demand. And Seagate says the 8TB Forge will launch at $699 for the 8TB drive, and $899 for the 20TB option. That's a lot of money for a drive you need to also put your own M.2 SSD into for it to function.

We'll also need to do more testing with things like game load times before passing judgment on the FireCuda Forge. But it likely makes much more sense in the 20TB capacity, where no single-drive consumer SSD-based option exists. At 8TB, there are options like SanDisk's Desk drive, which has a slower 10GBps interface, but is a full-fledged SSD, rather than a hard drive with some fast SSD cache. Surprisingly, that Sandisk drive is still on sale for $999. And unless you happen to have an old M.2 SSD lying around to install into the Forge, its price, including the SSD it needs to function, isn't going to be far off traditional solid-state options.

#10183. Fitbit Sense & Versa losing 3rd-party watch faces this month, existing downloads remain

Google announced today that Fitbit Sense and Versa smartwatches will soon lose the ability to “install or update third-party apps and clocks.”

This change to the Fitbit App Gallery applies to the Versa, Versa 2, Versa 3, Versa 4, Sense, and Sense 2.

Existing “third-party apps or clock faces installed on your Fitbit device” will remain available, but you can no longer download new ones (or update them) starting November 28. As such, “if you choose to delete an app or clock face, or factory reset your device, you will no longer be able to re-install it.”

Instead, the Fitbit App Gallery will “exclusively feature apps and clock faces created by Fitbit and Google.”

The November 28 deadline also applies to third-party developers. Google will “no longer support uploading new apps and clock faces or updating existing ones.”

Google winding down Fitbit OS for smartwatches is not particularly surprising as the company has been all-in on Wear OS and the Pixel Watch. That said, the Sense 2 and Versa 4 should probably no longer be on sale.

#10181. Open Responses: What you need to know

Open Responses is a new and open inference standard. Initiated by OpenAI, built by the open source AI community, and backed by the Hugging Face ecosystem, Open Responses is based on the Responses API and is designed for the future of Agents. In this blog post, we’ll look at how Open Responses works and why the open source community should use Open Responses.

The era of the chatbot is long gone, and agents dominate inference workloads. Developers are shifting toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act over long-time horizons. Despite this shift, much of the ecosystem still uses the Chat Completion format, which was designed for turn-based conversations and falls short for agentic use cases. The Responses format was designed to address these limitations, but it is closed and not as widely adopted. The Chat Completion format is still the de facto standard despite the alternatives.

This mismatch between the agentic workflow requirements and entrenched interfaces motivates the need for an open inference standard. Over the coming months, we will collaborate with the community and inference providers to implement and adapt Open Responses to a shared format, practically capable of replacing chat completions.

Open Responses builds on the direction OpenAI has set with their Responses API launched in March 2025, which superseded the existing Completion and Assistants APIs with a consistent way to:

Open Responses extends and open-sources the Responses API, making it more accessible for builders and routing providers to interoperate and collaborate on shared interests.

We’ll briefly explore the core changes that impact most community members. If you want to deep dive into the specification, check out the Open Responses documentation.

Client requests to Open Responses are similar to the existing Responses API. Below we demonstrate a request to the Open Responses API using curl. We're calling a proxy endpoint that routes to Inference Providers using the Open Responses API schema.

Clients that already support the Responses API can migrate to Open Responses with relatively little effort. The main changes involve how reasoning content is exposed:

OpenAI models used to only expose summary and encrypted_content. With Open Responses, providers may expose their raw reasoning via the API. Clients migrating from providers that previously returned only summaries and encrypted content will now have the opportunity to receive and handle raw reasoning streams when supported by their chosen provider.

For Model Providers, implementing the changes for Open Responses should be straightforward if they already adhere to the Responses API specification. For Routers, there is now the opportunity to standardize on a consistent endpoint and support configuration options for customization where needed.

Over time, as Providers continue to innovate, certain features will become standardized in the base specification.

In summary, migrating to Open Responses will make the inference experience more consistent and improve quality as undocumented extensions, interpretations, and workarounds of the legacy Completions API are normalized in Open Responses.

You can see how to stream reasoning chunks below.

Here’s the difference between getting an Open Response and using OpenAI Responses for reasoning deltas:

Open Responses distinguishes between “Model Providers” — those who provide inference — and “Routers” — intermediaries who orchestrate between multiple providers.

Clients can now specify a Provider along with provider-specific API options when making requests, allowing intermediary Routers to orchestrate requests between upstream providers.

Open Responses natively supports two categories of tools: internal and external. Externally hosted tools are implemented outside the model provider’s system. For example, client side functions to be executed, or MCP servers. Internally hosted tools are within the model provider’s system. For example, OpenAI’s file search or Google Drive integration. The model calls, executes, and retrieves results entirely within the provider's infrastructure, requiring no developer intervention.

Open Responses formalizes the agentic loop which is usually made up of a repeating cycle of reasoning, tool invocation, and response generation that enables models to autonomously complete multi-step tasks.

For internally-hosted tools, the provider manages the entire loop; executing tools, returning results to the model, and streaming output. This means that multi-step workflows like "search documents, summarize findings, then draft an email" use a single request.

Clients control loop behavior via max_tool_calls to cap iterations and tool_choice to constrain which tools are invocable:

The response contains all intermediate items: tool calls, results, reasoning.

Open Responses extends and improves the Responses API, providing richer and more detailed content definitions, compatibility, and deployment options. It also provides a standard way to execute sub-agent loops during primary inference calls, opening up powerful capabilities for AI Applications. We are looking forward to working with the Open Responses team and the community at large on future development of the specification.

You can try Open Responses with Hugging Face Inference Providers today. We have an early access version available for use on Hugging Face Spaces - try it with your Client and Open Responses Compliance Tool today!

Use Open Responses with Hugging Face Inference Providers

#10176. Introducing Waypoint-1: Real-time interactive video diffusion from Overworld

Overworld Stream: https://overworld.stream

Waypoint-1 is Overworld’s real-time-interactive video diffusion model, controllable and prompted via text, mouse, and keyboard. You can give the model some frames, run the model, and have it create a world you can step into and interact with.

The backbone of the model is a frame-causal rectified flow transformer trained on 10,000 hours of diverse video game footage paired with control inputs and text captions. Waypoint-1 is a latent model, meaning that it is trained on compressed frames.

The standard among existing world models has become taking pre-trained video models and fine-tuning them with brief and simplified control inputs. In contrast, Waypoint-1 is trained from the get-go with a focus on interactive experiences. With other models, controls are simple: you can move and rotate the camera once every few frames, with severe latency issues. With Waypoint-1 you are not limited at all as far as controls are concerned. You can move the camera freely with the mouse, and input any key on the keyboard, and all this with zero latency. Each frame is generated with your controls as context. Additionally, the model runs fast enough to provide a seamless experience even on consumer hardware.

Waypoint-1 was pre-trained via diffusion forcing, a technique with which the model learns to denoise future frames given past frames. A causal attention mask is applied such that a token in any given frame can only attend to tokens in its own frame, or past frames, but not future frames. Each frame is noised randomly, and as such the model learns to denoise each frame separately. During inference, you can then denoise new frames one at a time, allowing you to generate a procedural stream of new frames.

While diffusion forcing presents a strong baseline, randomly noising all frames is misaligned with a frame-by-frame autoregressive rollout. This inference mismatch results in error accumulation, and noisy long rollouts. To address this problem we post-train with self forcing, a technique that trains the model to produce realistic outputs under a regime which matches inference behavior. Self-forcing via DMD has the added benefit of one-pass CFG, and few-step denoising.

WorldEngine is Overworld’s high‑performance inference library for interactive world model streaming. It provides the core tooling for building inference applications in pure Python, optimized for low latency, high throughput, extensibility, and developer simplicity. The runtime loop is designed for interactivity: it consumes context frame images, keyboard/mouse inputs, and text, and outputs image frames for real‑time streaming.

On Waypoint‑1‑Small (2.3B) running on a 5090, WorldEngine sustains ~30,000 token‑passes/sec (single denoising pass; 256 tokens per frame) and achieves 30 FPS at 4 steps or 60 FPS at 2 steps

#10175. Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

LangSmith is closed-source and restricts self-hosting to enterprise licenses, teams that run their own LLMOps stack and want to keep traces on their own servers need an alternative. To find the best fit, we set a baseline by tracing a small TypeScript agent (equipped with two tools) in LangSmith Cloud. Then, we ran the exact same agent through Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Opik, and AcruxCore using each platform's recommended TypeScript setup. All tests were run on November 5, 2026, and we pulled every trace back through each tool's API to verify the data.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree for the test prompt: a single agent span containing three LLM calls and two tool calls. The real differences between them come down to how much boilerplate code you have to write, how spans are typed, whether costs are tracked, and the overall server footprint.

Why Teams Look for a LangSmith Alternative

LangSmith remains the best choice if you already use LangChain and allow cloud hosting—it required just 25 lines of code in our test. The alternatives below are for teams that don't fit that profile.

To test these platforms, we built a simple customer support agent equipped with two tools:

Both tools use static fixture data to ensure every test run is identical. The agent runs a standard loop: it prompts the model, executes any requested tools, and stops once the model provides a final answer.

We tested the agent with three specific prompts to see how the tracing handled different levels of complexity:

For our comparison, we focused entirely on the third question because it generates a robust, multi-step trace.

Under the hood, the agent uses the standard openai package to call the qwen3.8-flash model. We originally picked this model based on its reliable tool-calling behavior during early probing thought it once skipped a tool call later.

We used LangSmith as our baseline. By tracing the agent there first, we created a checklist of every field it captured, and we judged all the alternatives against that exact list.

For setup, we followed the recommended TypeScript approach from each tool's documentation. Phoenix didn't have specific instructions for using its register() helper with OpenAI in TypeScript, so we adapted the pattern from their Anthropic guide.

Here is the agent with no tracing. Each tool section adds one tracing file that imports these files and changes nothing in them.

LangSmith traces the plain openai package with two helpers. wrapOpenAI records each model call, and traceable records your own functions. Without traceable on the run and the tools, wrapOpenAI alone gave three separate root runs and no tool runs.

This file adds 25 lines and removes 3, and installs one package.

LangSmith showed one root run with five children in call order: LLM, get_order_status, LLM, get_refund_policy, LLM. Every field it recorded became a row of the checklist table under "Results". Cost appeared only after a custom price entry. In our error run the failing tool was marked as an error, but the root stayed success: traceable turned the throw into a rejected promise that our agent did not await, so the agent carried on and answered.

Langfuse self-hosts as six containers, including ClickHouse, a column store built for large scans. In our measurement the stack held 2.60–2.64 GiB of memory at idle. Its Docker Compose guide recommends at least 4 CPU cores and 16 GiB RAM, with about 100 GiB of disk.

The TypeScript path is built on OpenTelemetry. You start the OTel Node SDK with LangfuseSpanProcessor, wrap the client with observeOpenAI, and wrap your own functions with observe:

This file adds 31 lines and removes 5, and installs four packages. We pinned the OTel Node SDK to 0.223.0, because @langfuse/otel 6.1.1 does not accept 0.300.0.

Langfuse successfully recreated the same trace tree, neatly tagging the spans as AGENT, GENERATION, and TOOL. It captured all the essentials: tool calls, tool definitions, and the complete message history. However, for the LLM output, it only saved the assistant's message—dropping the finish_reason, response ID, and the provider name.

We ran our deployment in Langfuse v4's events_only mode, which turns off the v1 trace endpoint. Because of this, the API didn't return a centralized trace object or root-level sums for tokens and costs, even though the UI calculated and displayed them perfectly (we didn't test other modes).

Costs showed up exactly as expected once we added a custom price entry. Since Langfuse calculates prices based on the specific usage types you define, and we only set rates for input and output, the separate reasoning tokens went unpriced. Finally, during our error test, the observe wrapper let the error bubble up to the agent, correctly flagging both the tool and the root span as an ERROR.

Phoenix self-hosts as two containers, one Python server and Postgres. In our measurement it held 0.47 GiB at idle. Phoenix is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0, so it is not open source. Authentication is off until you turn it on.

The TypeScript path uses Phoenix's register() helper and the OpenInference instrumentation for the OpenAI package. OpenInference is a set of OpenTelemetry attribute names for LLM spans. traceAgent and traceTool wrap the run and the tools:

This file adds 32 lines and removes 3, and installs three packages.

Phoenix rebuilt the same tree, typed as AGENT, LLM and TOOL. Each LLM span keeps the full OpenAI response object, plus the messages as flattened attributes. The root span stores no token count, but Phoenix computes a sum for the root and the trace when you read it. Cost and those sums are only in the GraphQL API and the UI, and the REST API has no per-trace endpoint.

Cost appeared after a custom price entry under Settings > Models, and Phoenix priced the reasoning tokens by falling back to the output price. In the error run, the tool span and the root were marked ERROR, and the tool span carried an exception event with the stack trace.

Opik self-hosts as eight containers, including ClickHouse, MySQL and ZooKeeper. In our measurement it held 3.69 GiB at idle, the most of the four. The self-hosted UI opened without a login, so every trace was readable from any machine that could reach the port.

The TypeScript path wraps the client with trackOpenAI and your own functions with track. By default trackOpenAI starts a new trace for every model call, so the file passes the run's span through the documented parent option:

This file adds 33 lines and removes 5. It installs opik-openai 2.2.142, and npm adds opik 1.11.14 as its peer, because opik-openai asks for opik ^1.8.61.

Opik successfully recreated the trace tree, and its trace object neatly tallies token counts across all LLM spans. In the logs, tool arguments are bundled into an array, and the LLM output only retains the assistant's message.

We did notice a quirk with the documented OpenAI wrapper (tested on the npm package opik 1.11.14): it tags model calls as general rather than llm, which incorrectly leaves the llm_span_count at zero. (We didn't test newer Opik core versions to see if this has changed). Additionally, because our synchronous tools execute in under a millisecond, they log the exact same start time as the subsequent LLM call, causing the UI to list the LLM call first out of order.

Cost tracking is entirely manual. Opik showed no costs by default, and the documentation doesn't mention a custom price table. We checked the configuration tabs on our 2.2.52 instance (Feedback definitions, AI Providers, Workspace preferences) and found no model pricing settings. To see costs, you have to manually assign a price to each individual span yourself—only the spans we hardcoded this way displayed a cost.

Finally, error reporting is highly detailed. If something fails, Opik attaches an error_info block—complete with the error type, message, and full traceback—directly to the tool span, the root span, and the overall trace.

AcruxCore self-hosts as five containers: Postgres, Redis, a Node API and worker, and nginx. In our measurement it held 0.39 GiB at idle, the least of the four. Its quickstart leaves sign-up open and ships a committed default GATEWAY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, which encrypts stored provider keys; replace it. We tested a local build from 2026-09-17.

The TypeScript path AcruxCore's docs put first is its gateway. The official openai client keeps working: you point its baseURL at ACRUXCORE_BASE_URL + "/gateway" and call a model registered in AcruxCore, which forwards each call to an OpenAI-compatible provider. The gateway records every model call as an llm span. The SDK's step helpers add the rest: traces.step opens the agent span, traces.wrap wraps each tool, and two headers file the gateway's spans under the agent span:

This file adds 30 lines and removes 5, and installs one package. It builds its own client, so it does not use provider.ts. The gateway refused our team API key, so the client uses a gateway virtual key created in the dashboard.

On this path every model call passes through the AcruxCore server, which none of the other four tools need. If you do not want a proxy in the request path, the SDK's register() helper sends OpenTelemetry spans from your process instead. On that path the step helpers do not join the openai package's spans, so you write the agent and tool spans by hand.

AcruxCore rebuilt the same tree, typed as agent, llm and tool, in call order. Each LLM span keeps the full response, the provider and the cached-token count, and the trace carries a token total. The LLM spans do not keep the tool definitions sent to the model, and no reasoning-token count was recorded. The trace took its name from the question, not from the agent span, and each LLM span is named by its start time.

Cost appeared on every LLM span and as a sum on the trace, from the custom price we set on the model in AcruxCore's model list. In the error run, the step helpers marked the tool span and the agent root as error with the error message, with no status code of ours. The API returned no stack trace.

All five tools accept traces over OTLP, the OpenTelemetry wire format. trace-otel.ts sends the same spans with no vendor package: the OTel Node SDK, the OTLP/HTTP protobuf exporter and the OpenInference OpenAI instrumentation. The exporter reads its endpoint and headers from environment variables:

We ran the two-tool question once per backend and changed only environment variables: the endpoint, the headers, and for Phoenix a resource attribute that sets the project name (without it, spans go to a default project). "Accepted" means the exporter reported success, which it does only for an HTTP 2xx, and we read the spans back through each API.

Opik stored the root and tool spans as general although AGENT and TOOL kinds were sent; the cause is Not tested. LangSmith mapped AGENT to its chain type. If you instrument with plain OTel and OpenInference attributes, your raw spans are not tied to one vendor, but span types, cost and trace views still differ by backend.

The first table covers setup: how much server each tool needs, how much code we changed in the agent, and how cost and the plain OTel exporter worked. Phoenix and AcruxCore had the smallest servers, and AcruxCore needed the fewest lines among the self-hosted tools. Opik was the only one without a price table.

The second table checks each trace against what LangSmith recorded for the same run, one field at a time. All five rebuilt the same tree with tokens and durations. They differ in span types, how much of the LLM output they keep, where token sums live, and how much detail they store for the failing tool.

Token totals for the two-tool question ranged from 1,910 to 2,111. Each tool traced a separate run and reasoning length varies, so these numbers do not compare the tools.

All five tools successfully traced our test agent, so the right choice really comes down to your team's specific constraints, infrastructure preferences, and how tracing fits into the rest of your MLOps tooling.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree. The real deciding factors are boilerplate code, span typing, cost tracking, and server bloat.

LangSmith remains the simplest option for LangChain users who can utilize the cloud. Otherwise, your choice depends on your priorities: Langfuse for community size, Phoenix for a lightweight Postgres footprint, Opik for strict Apache-2.0 compliance with deep error logging, or AcruxCore for combined tracing and tool governance on minimal hardware. Best of all, if you stick to standard OpenTelemetry spans, you aren't locked in—you can try them all and easily pivot later.

#10174. Samsung Galaxy S27 series camera specs leak, and they’re disappointing

New leaks reveal the camera specs for Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series which includes three lenses across the lineup, but not the upgrades you want, nor what Ultra owners might expect.

SammyGuru reports that Samsung is “evaluating” camera setups for the Galaxy S27, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra, and it looks like a mixed bag across the board.

The base Galaxy S27 and S27+ are looking very familiar, with identical main camera sensors to last year, and the same ultrawide sensor that’s been in use since the Galaxy S23 series. The telephoto and selfie sensors are looking at new hardware, but without any major spec upgrades.

Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, meanwhile, have a new 200MP main camera on deck, a 50MP ultrawide shooter, and a mere 12MP telephoto. The Ultra might get 5x compared to the Pro’s 3x optical zoom, but with a secondary telephoto lens going missing, existing users of the lineup are sure to be disappointed.

Notably, SammyGuru’s article mentions the Pro as using “the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 3x sensor,” but shows the 12MP Samsung S5K3LD in that place instead. We’re assuming that’s a typo seeing as the post mentions the Pro as using the Samsung S5KJN3 or the Sony IMX855 earlier on, but regardless, the Pro only gets 3x optical zoom to the Ultra’s 5x.

Some of these specs have been mentioned by other sources such as GalaxyClub and leaker Ice Universe, but this is the most complete picture of the S27’s camera plans we’ve seen to date.

Personally, I’m very “whelmed” on this one. As RAMageddon rages on and Samsung hunts for new ways to balance specs vs price, cameras are a place that’s obviously going to be cut, but competitors are already running laps around Samsung on the hardware front. Cutting lenses and skimping out on upgrades (again) doesn’t help matters.

#10171. AI Agents Are Moving Faster Than Trust: Why Security Needs A New Foundation

Dr. Pravir Malik is the founder and technologist of QIQuantum and the Forbes Technology Council Community leader for Quantum Computing.

Bruce Schneier’s enduring warning that “security is a process, not a product” remains right. But the next security stack must go further. It must make trust a property of architecture: what can be known, what can be exported, who may decide and what evidence must exist before action occurs.

The first is quantum risk. NIST finalized its first post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards in 2024 and urges organizations to begin migrating now. The concern extends beyond when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives. Migration can take years to complete, while adversaries can collect encrypted data today for “harvest now, decrypt later” attacks.

The second is agentic AI. Agents can interpret goals, invoke tools and initiate transactions or configuration changes at machine speed. NIST’s 2026 AI Agent Standards Initiative reflects the need for agents to act securely on behalf of users. Yet authentication alone does not establish authority. A valid agent using a valid credential can still exceed its purpose, scope, approval boundary or time window.

The third is evidentiary. Organizations often respond to uncertainty by exporting more logs, traces and attestation data. That may improve visibility, but repeated high-resolution evidence can also become a reconstruction channel. A compromised component may even help manufacture the narrative used to certify it.

Leading companies are addressing different parts of this problem.

Cloudflare reported in October 2025 that more than half of human-initiated traffic on its network was protected against harvest now, decrypt later attacks through post-quantum encryption. That demonstrates how quantum-safe migration can move from standards into Internet-scale infrastructure.

Microsoft’s Pluton security processor shows another direction. Integrating a secure cryptographic subsystem into the system-on-chip brings the hardware root of trust closer to the processor, reducing exposure from communication with a separate security component.

Agentic security is producing a third response. Microsoft Entra Agent ID gives AI agents purpose-built identities, governance and adaptive access controls. Okta similarly treats agents as first-class identities, using short-lived credentials, least-privilege policies and runtime control over tool connections.

These are serious advances. Together, they point toward quantum-resistant cryptography, stronger hardware anchors and disciplined agent authorization. But a missing layer remains: a common trust constitution connecting the physical root, the evidence surface and the authority to act.

Many security systems begin with something readable in principle: a private key, credential, device measurement or protected state. Hardware can make extraction extremely difficult, and cryptography can constrain misuse. Yet if the root becomes a transcript, it can potentially be copied, replayed or modeled.

In my Springer book, Pioneering Engineered Security in the Quantum-Cyber Era, I propose a different category of trust. The root would itself be a quantum object: a non-exportable physical imprint or relationship governed from the outset by quantum no-go laws. Hardware would embody this root, while its observable face would remain governed and deliberately incomplete. External systems would receive bounded receipts about health, freshness, lineage and continuing congruence rather than raw state or increasingly revealing diagnostics.

An independent witness would test continuity without sharing the actor’s narrative machinery. High-consequence action would require the complete evidence envelope to support it. This is a research and engineering trajectory, not a claim that a production-ready quantum trust chip already exists. Its importance lies in defining what such hardware must make structurally true.

The no-cloning theorem establishes that an arbitrary unknown quantum state cannot be perfectly copied. The no-broadcasting theorem extends this restriction to noncommuting mixed states.

These laws do not automatically make a device secure. Their value is that they can be translated into interface requirements. A trust root should have no universal readout path. Evidence should strengthen confidence without accumulating into tomography: a reconstruction of protected state. A counterfeit or tampered object should fail under fresh challenges because it cannot preserve the lawful relationship between protected interior and governed surface. The actor should not be its own sole witness.

The goal is not to hide a conventional secret more effectively. It is to arrange hardware and interfaces so that trust cannot naturally collapse into exportable data.

Agentic AI provides the clearest test of this architecture. The model may propose an action, but an enforcement plane outside the probabilistic model should decide whether that action is admissible now.

That decision should examine identity, credentials, declared purpose, target scope, current policy, approval boundaries, lifecycle state and independent evidence. Only a signed decision receipt bound to the approved action should release execution.

This builds on Zero Trust, which distinguishes authentication from authorization, by binding authority to the specific action and its current evidence. A valid identity must never substitute for valid authority.

PQC, hardware security processors, agent identity, least privilege and Zero Trust remain essential. But they address different parts of the problem. Individually, they cannot guarantee that a trust root never becomes a transcript, repeated verification never becomes a learning channel or a valid agent never exceeds its authority.

A deeper redesign would connect three principles: authority anchored in non-exportable physical structure; evidence limited to bounded, independently verifiable proofs; and high-consequence action released only when identity, purpose, policy, lifecycle continuity and current evidence align.

Designing this architecture cannot wait for mature hardware. Quantum migration is underway, encrypted information can be collected today and agentic systems are moving from recommendation toward action. The quantum transition therefore reaches beyond replacing RSA or elliptic-curve cryptography. It requires us to reconsider what creates authority, what counts as evidence and what must be proven before machines may act.

What we need now is a new category of trust on which the security stack can be rebuilt.

#10169. Differential Transformer V2

We introduce Differential Transformer V2 (DIFF V2), an improved version of Differential Transformer (DIFF V1). This revision focuses on inference efficiency, training stability for production-level LLMs, and architectural elegance.

We conduct pretraining experiments on production-scale LLMs, including dense models and a 30A3 MoE on trillions of tokens using large learning rate of 6e-4 to 1e-3. Experimental observations:

The experiments are still running. We expect to explore in later stages of training:

After the experiments complete and we evaluate the results, we will prepare a more formal report.

(For simplicity, we omit the batch dimension and assume that both the input and output of the following flash_attn_func are three-dimensional tensors (tokens, heads, head dimension). Heads belonging to the same GQA group are arranged contiguously in the output)

Note DIFF V2 subtracts two heads that are in the same GQA group, which means they share the same key and value. This is crucial to performance. See design ablations section and Github code.

Full code at: unilm/Diff-Transformer/Diff-Transformer-V2 at master · microsoft/unilm In the script, h represents number of query heads, h_kv represents number of key-value heads, and d means head dimension. The λ\lambdaλ in DIFF V2 is projected from XXX for each token each head.

DIFF V2 doubles number of query heads while maintaining number of key value heads, and the extra dimension is reduced back to h*d after the differential operation so the WOW_OWO​ projection remains the same as baseline Transformer.

DIFF V2 introduces additional query heads compared to the baseline Transformer, but does not increase the number of key-value (KV) heads. Since LLM decoding is typically memory-bound, this design allows DIFF V2 to achieve decoding speeds on par with standard Transformer. Besides, since head dimension is aligned between query, key and value, there is no need for custom attention kernels for DIFF V2. In contrast, DIFF V1 can be slower during decoding because the value cache must be loaded twice, and a custom attention kernel is needed. DIFF V2 can also increase the arithmetic intensity of the attention module during decoding.

During pretraining, when using cutting-edge FlashAttention kernels on H-series and B-series GPUs, the throughput reduction introduced by DIFF V2 is negligible. For long-sequence prefilling, we recommend combining DIFF V2 with techniques such as YOCO (also used in Gemma 3n), which already reduces prefilling complexity to linear time with respect to sequence length.

An alternative perspective is to compare DIFF V2 with a Transformer that has the same query dimension 2h*d. Under this comparison, both models exhibit same attention kernel speed, while DIFF V2 has less parameters and flops in output projection.

In the standard Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA), let Q,K,V∈Rn×dQ, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}Q,K,V∈Rn×d be the queries, keys, and values. The context vector CCC is defined as:

C=Softmax(QKTd)V=AV C = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V = AV C=Softmax(d​QKT​)V=AV

Where A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n is the attention weight matrix. Let's focus on a single row of CCC, denoted as ci\mathbf{c}_ici​, which is a weighted sum of value vectors vj\mathbf{v}_jvj​:

A typical phenomenon is that when DIFF V1 is pre-trained at a large learning rate, the gradient norm experiences a larger increase compared to Transformer in the later stages, along with higher variance. We adopted the per-head RMSNorm design in DIFF V1 primarily because of the doubled value head dimension and the globally shared λ\lambdaλ across all tokens. Given the modifications made to these two aspects in DIFF V2, we found that removing RMSNorm is now safe.

We conduct pretraining experiments on production-scale LLMs, including dense models and a 30A3 MoE on trillions of tokens using large learning rate of 6e-4 to 1e-3.

The experiments are still running. What we have observed now:

We expect to explore in later stages of training:

In theory, a standard Transformer with 2h2h2h attention heads can learn the differential operation by learning WO2i=−WO2i+1,i=0,1,…,h−1W_O^{2i}=-W_O^{2i+1}, i=0,1,\ldots,h-1WO2i​=−WO2i+1​,i=0,1,…,h−1, where WOiW_O^{i}WOi​ denotes the output projection of head iii, and head 2i2i2i and 2i+12i+12i+1 belong to the same GQA group.

Assumption 1. In practice, such a solution is difficult to learn through optimization, as it requires two sets of parameters to converge to exact negatives of each other.

Assumption 2. The differential operation can be learned by the model and the model chooses to learn it in the training. Then explicitly constructing it before the output projection as in DIFF V2 can save half of the WOW_OWO​ parameters. The number of saved parameters is also non-trivial. Under the current GQA setting, the parameters in the attention module are dominated by WQW_QWQ​ and WOW_OWO​; Therefore, approximately 25% of the attention-module parameters can be saved. The saved parameter budget can then be reallocated to other parts of the model.

Even if DIFF V2, after reallocating parameters, does not achieve a lower loss than the baseline but merely matches it, the method is still worthwhile if it provides additional benefits such as improved training stability, better control of outliers, or higher training efficiency. This is analogous to GQA, which matches the loss of MHA while reducing KV-cache as an additional benefit. So the key question becomes empirical performance.

(For simplicity, we omit the batch dimension and assume that both the input and output of the following flash_attn_func are three-dimensional tensors (tokens, heads, head dimension). Heads belonging to the same GQA group are arranged contiguously in the output)

In our large learning rate setting, the ablation 1 setting exhibits obvious training instability (much more loss and gradient spikes) and higher loss comparing to DIFF V2. The value should be shared in the two subtraction heads to construct differential operation, as discussed in DIFF V1 paper.

Both ablation 2 and ablation 3 lead to higher language modeling loss than DIFF V2. Ablation 2 maintains training stability similar to DIFF V2, whereas ablation 3 is less stable (still more stable than ablation 1).

Ablation 4 also has higher training loss comparing to DIFF V2.

This is a fascinating and thorough update on the Differential Transformer architecture. The transition from DIFF V1 to V2 addresses some critical practical hurdles in a very elegant way.

The key design choice of doubling query heads within shared GQA groups is clever. It successfully decouples the innovative "differential" attention operation from the need for custom kernels, making it a much more viable drop-in replacement for standard attention. The analysis of how this design overcomes the softmax magnitude constraint and helps eliminate attention sinks is particularly convincing.

The reported early results—lower loss, reduced gradient spikes, and better control of activation outliers, especially at large learning rates—are highly promising. It suggests DIFF V2 isn't just a parameter-saving trick but may offer fundamental improvements in training dynamics and stability.

I have a couple of questions out of curiosity:

Long-Context Performance: You mention exploring "context rot" alleviation in later stages. Given the modified attention output dynamics, do you have any early hypotheses on whether DIFF V2 might inherently improve performance on very long sequences compared to a baseline Transformer with similar parameter budgets?

Broader Application: The principle seems powerful yet simple. Beyond the dense and MoE models tested here, do you see potential for applying this differential attention mechanism in other architectures, like state-space models or multimodal transformers?
