#10073. How to Reduce Hallucinations in LLMs

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

In this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

An LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process says "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

Newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

Northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:

The traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:

Every version calls the model through one small helper:

We're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

Opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply said it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:

It treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:

Northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

The model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:

Right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:

Delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data says nothing about price matching:

It said it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

If version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

Version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:

Zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

The model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

If all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:

Every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

The last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

Third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:

It's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:

If a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

It's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

This script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:

The check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:

Version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:

No model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

It cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

Not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

Collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:

The model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.

#10071. LeRobot v0.5.0: Scaling Every Dimension

With over 200 merged PRs and over 50 new contributors since v0.4.0, LeRobot v0.5.0 is our biggest release yet — expanding in every direction at once. More robots (including our first humanoid), more policies (including the comeback of autoregressive VLAs), faster datasets, simulation environments you can load straight from the Hub, and a modernized codebase running on Python 3.12 and Transformers v5. Whether you're training policies in simulation or deploying them on real hardware, v0.5.0 has something for you.

LeRobot v0.5.0 adds full Unitree G1 humanoid support (whole-body control models), new policies –including Pi0-FAST autoregressive VLAs and Real-Time Chunking for responsive inference–, and streaming video encoding that eliminates wait times between recording episodes. The release also introduces EnvHub for loading simulation environments from the Hugging Face Hub, NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena integration, and a major codebase modernization with Python 3.12+, Transformers v5, and third-party policy plugins.

LeRobot v0.5.0 dramatically expands the roster of supported hardware — from arms and mobile robots to a full humanoid.

The biggest hardware addition in this release: full Unitree G1 humanoid support. This is LeRobot's first humanoid integration, and it's comprehensive:

The G1 integration represents a major step toward general-purpose robotics within LeRobot — moving beyond tabletop arms into full-body embodied AI. Try it out yourself by following the documentation.

We've added support for the OpenArm robot and its companion OpenArm Mini teleoperator. OpenArm is a capable robot arm with full LeRobot integration, and the Mini serves as its natural teleoperation device. Both support bi-manual configurations, enabling dual-arm setups for more complex manipulation tasks. Check it out in the documentation.

New motor controller support via CAN (Controller Area Network) bus opens the door to higher-performance actuators:

These additions mean LeRobot can now drive a wider variety of professional-grade actuators beyond the existing Dynamixel and Feetech ecosystem.

This release brings six new policies and techniques into LeRobot, pushing the boundaries of what's possible with open-source robot learning.

Pi0-FAST brings autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models to LeRobot with FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization). Unlike the flow-matching approach of Pi0, Pi0-FAST uses an autoregressive action expert (based on Gemma 300M) that generates discretized action tokens, enabling:

Real-Time Chunking is an inference-time technique from Physical Intelligence that makes flow-matching policies dramatically more responsive. Instead of waiting for a full action chunk to finish before replanning, RTC continuously blends new predictions with in-progress actions, producing smoother and more reactive behavior.

RTC is not a standalone policy — it's an enhancement that plugs into existing flow-matching policies (Pi0 family, SmolVLA & Diffusion). Configure it via --policy.rtc_config.enabled=true.

This is a game-changer for real-world deployment where latency matters. Read the original paper for the technical details and our documentation.

Wall-X is a new VLA policy built on Qwen2.5-VL with flow-matching action prediction. It combines the strong vision-language understanding of Qwen2.5-VL with a flow-matching head for cross-embodiment robotic control.

X-VLA brings a Florence2-based VLA to LeRobot. Built on Microsoft's Florence-2 vision-language model, X-VLA offers an alternative backbone for VLA policies, expanding the diversity of foundation models available for robot learning. Check out the training guide for setup instructions and the base model.

SARM (Stage-Aware Reward Modeling) tackles one of the hardest problems in robot learning: long-horizon tasks. Instead of using a single global linear progress signal over the whole episode, it models progress in a stage-aware manner by predicting both the task stage and the progress within that stage. This makes it much easier to train policies for complex, multi-step manipulation tasks. Start experimenting with it by following the documentation.

You can now fine-tune large VLAs using LoRA (and other PEFT methods) without modifying the core training pipeline. PEFT configuration lives at the policy level, making it straightforward to adapt massive foundation models to your specific robot and task with a fraction of the compute. Learn more reading the documentation.

The dataset pipeline gets major performance improvements in this release, making both data collection and training significantly faster.

Previously, recording a dataset meant waiting after each episode for video encoding to finish. No more. With streaming video encoding, frames are encoded in real-time as they're captured — meaning zero wait time between episodes. Just finish one episode and immediately start the next.

Streaming encoding also supports hardware encoder auto-detection, so if your system has a GPU-accelerated video encoder, LeRobot will use it automatically:

Streaming encoding performance can vary significantly depending on your hardware and recording setup (number of cameras, resolution, etc.). Make sure to review the streaming video encoding documentation before enabling it.

Under the hood, we've fixed key data access bottlenecks and overhauled image processing:

The dataset editing toolkit continues to grow:

EnvHub is a new way to use simulation environments in LeRobot: load them directly from the Hugging Face Hub. Instead of installing environment packages locally and wiring up registration, you can now point LeRobot at a Hub repository and it handles everything — downloading the environment code, registering it with Gymnasium, and making it available for training and evaluation.

Hub environments use HubEnvConfig, which downloads and executes remote make_env functions:

This lowers the barrier for sharing custom simulation environments with the community. Package your environment, push it to the Hub, and anyone can train on it. Check out the documentation to learn more. Here's an example to get started: LeIsaac x LeRobot EnvHub tutorial.

We've integrated NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, bringing GPU-accelerated simulation to LeRobot. IsaacLab-Arena provides a collection of manipulation tasks running on NVIDIA's Isaac Sim, offering massively parallel environment instances for fast reinforcement learning. The integration includes dedicated pre/post-processing steps and full compatibility with LeRobot's training pipeline. Check out the documentation.

Beyond these headline features, v0.5.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, CI/CD enhancements, and quality-of-life improvements across the entire codebase. From better type checking to more robust test infrastructure, we're investing in the foundations that make LeRobot reliable and maintainable as it scales.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community — contributors, users, and collaborators alike — for helping LeRobot grow into what it is today. Every bug report, PR, and discussion makes this project better.

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️

There's a big surprise coming just right around the corner, stay tuned! 👕

#10069. Ulysses Sequence Parallelism: Training with Million-Token Contexts

Training large language models on long sequences has become essential for building capable AI systems. As models are increasingly used for tasks like document analysis, code understanding, complex reasoning, and RAG workloads, the need to process sequences of hundreds of thousands—or even millions—of tokens has grown dramatically. To put this in perspective, an average book is roughly 250k tokens, so training on multi-document contexts or book-length inputs requires handling sequences well beyond what fits on a single GPU. However, training with such long contexts presents significant memory challenges: the attention computation scales quadratically with sequence length, quickly exceeding GPU memory for contexts beyond tens of thousands of tokens.

Ulysses Sequence Parallelism (part of the Arctic Long Sequence Training (ALST) protocol from Snowflake AI Research) provides an elegant solution by distributing the attention computation across multiple GPUs through attention head parallelism. In this post, we'll explore how Ulysses works and how it's been integrated across the Hugging Face ecosystem—from Accelerate to the Transformers Trainer and TRL's SFTTrainer.

The attention mechanism in transformers scales quadratically with sequence length. For a sequence of length n n n, standard attention requires O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) FLOPs and O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) memory to compute and store the attention score matrix. Optimized implementations like FlashAttention reduce the memory to O(n) O(n) O(n) by tiling the computation and never materializing the full attention matrix—but the O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2) compute remains. For very long sequences (32k+ tokens), even with FlashAttention, training still pushes the limits of single-GPU memory.

Consider these scenarios where long-context training is essential:

Traditional data parallelism doesn't help here—each GPU still needs to process the full sequence inside the attention block. We need a way to split the sequence itself across multiple devices.

Ulysses Sequence Parallelism (SP), introduced in the DeepSpeed Ulysses paper, takes a clever approach: in addition to splitting on the sequence dimension, it also partitions the attention heads across GPUs.

Sequence Sharding: The input sequence is split along the sequence dimension across P P P GPUs. Each GPU i i i holds tokens [i⋅n/P,(i+1)⋅n/P) [i \cdot n/P, (i+1) \cdot n/P) [i⋅n/P,(i+1)⋅n/P).

QKV Projection: Each GPU computes the query, key, and value projections for its local sequence chunk.

All-to-All Communication: An all-to-all collective operation redistributes the data so that each GPU holds all sequence positions after the projections, but only for a subset of attention heads.

Local Attention: Each GPU computes attention for its assigned heads using standard attention mechanisms (FlashAttention or SDPA).

All-to-All Communication: Another all-to-all operation reverses the redistribution, returning to sequence-sharded format.

Output Projection: Each GPU computes the output projection for its local sequence chunk.

The key insight is that attention heads are independent—each head can be computed separately. By trading sequence locality for head locality, Ulysses enables efficient parallelization with relatively low communication overhead.

Ulysses requires two all-to-all operations per attention layer, with total communication volume of O(n⋅d/P) O(n \cdot d / P) O(n⋅d/P) per GPU, where:

Ring Attention communicates O(n⋅d) O(n \cdot d) O(n⋅d) per GPU — a factor of P P P more — via P−1 P-1 P−1 sequential point-to-point transfers around the ring. Ulysses also benefits from lower latency because all-to-all can exploit full bisectional bandwidth in a single collective step, whereas Ring Attention serializes over P−1 P-1 P−1 hops.

Accelerate provides the foundation for Ulysses sequence parallelism through its ParallelismConfig class and DeepSpeed integration.

When you call accelerator.prepare(), Ulysses is automatically set up:

With Ulysses, each GPU computes loss on different parts of the sequence. The losses must be aggregated properly, weighted by the number of valid tokens per rank. If you're using the Transformers Trainer or TRL's SFTTrainer, this is handled automatically—the code below is only needed when writing a custom Accelerate training loop:

The weighted loss aggregation ensures correct gradients when tokens are unevenly distributed across ranks (e.g., when some ranks contain only padding or masked out prompt tokens).

Both Ulysses and Ring Attention use position_ids instead of attention_mask for causal masking during training. A 4D attention mask at these sequence lengths would be just as prohibitive as the attention scores themselves—at 128k tokens, that's another ~1TB tensor. Position IDs achieve the same causal behavior with O(n) O(n) O(n) memory instead of O(n2) O(n^2) O(n2). During evaluation/inference, DeepSpeed's SP attention layer can bypass the SP operations entirely (via disable_in_eval) and fall back to the model's default attention implementation.

The Transformers Trainer provides seamless Ulysses integration through TrainingArguments.parallelism_config. It handles all the SP-specific details automatically—dataloader wrapping, sequence sharding, and loss aggregation—so you don't need to write any of the custom loss code shown above.

Just pass the same parallelism_config from above into TrainingArguments:

Dataloader Wrapping: After model preparation, the Trainer wraps the dataloader with UlyssesSPDataLoaderAdapter

Loss Computation: The compute_loss method detects SP mode and routes to specialized _deepspeed_sp_compute_loss which handles:

Batch Size Calculation: The effective data parallel world size accounts for SP:

Dataloader Length Adjustment: Training step calculations are adjusted for SP's effect on iteration count

Use an accelerate config file or command-line arguments:

TRL's SFTTrainer builds on the Transformers Trainer and adds specific optimizations for supervised fine-tuning with long sequences.

The SFTTrainer automatically handles pre-shifted labels when Ulysses is enabled:

Both Ulysses and Ring Attention enable long-context training, but they have different characteristics:

Since switching between the two only requires changing the accelerate config, we recommend trying both and comparing performance and memory usage on your specific setup. The main constraint is that Ulysses requires num_heads >= sp_size, while Ring Attention has no such limitation.

Always ensure your sequence length is divisible by sp_size:

Flash Attention 2 provides cleaner output and better performance than SDPA:

Use Flash Attention 3 for Hopper and look out for Flash Attention 4 release for Blackwell (FA2 on Blackwell is quite slow).

For very large models, combine Ulysses with ZeRO Stage 3:

If the model is huge, you can offload the params as well by adding to the above:

This environment variable will allow for a longer sequence length:

Remember: dp_replicate_size × dp_shard_size × sp_size = num_processes

If your desired model architecture is supported by Liger-Kernel, it is fully compatible with Ulysses SP and can be enabled with a single flag:

The main memory saving comes from FusedLinearCrossEntropy which avoids materializing the full logits tensor during loss calculation. The savings grow with longer sequences where the logits tensor is larger.

Additionally, you can enable TiledMLP to further extend sequence length — like FusedLinearCrossEntropy, it saves working memory by tiling large matrix operations.

You don't need to worry about manually balancing tokens across SP ranks—the loss aggregation code handles uneven distributions gracefully (including ranks with zero valid tokens). With random batching over a reasonably sized dataset, the distribution evens out statistically over training.

To quantify the benefits of Ulysses SP, we trained Qwen3-4B on the Gutenberg English streaming dataset using TRL's SFTTrainer. All experiments ran on H100 80GB GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, CPU optimizer offloading, gradient checkpointing, and flash-attn2 as the attention backend.

The benchmark runs in the table above use the same global batch size (8 micro-batches), cosine learning-rate schedule, and seed, so those benchmark loss curves are directly comparable.

To verify SP-vs-DP loss equivalence, we ran controlled 4-GPU A/B experiments with identical seed, model, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and data order.

For fair comparison, GAS must scale with SP:

Measured over 20 steps on 4 GPUs in controlled equivalence harnesses:

Takeaway: under matched token budget, SP and non-SP match on canonical token-normalized loss. The remaining difference is in trainer-reported logging (loss), not in the underlying cross-entropy objective.

At 8K tokens, DP=4 and SP=4 use nearly the same memory per GPU (~22 GB with ZeRO-3). The advantage of SP is that it enables scaling to much longer sequences: at 96K tokens (12x longer), peak memory is 66 GB — still within the H100's 80 GB capacity. At 128K, the model OOMs, establishing the practical limit for this configuration. DP=4 without SP cannot scale beyond 8K for this model.

At the same sequence length (8K), SP=4 has comparable throughput to the single-GPU baseline — the all-to-all communication overhead is minimal on NVLink-connected GPUs. The real benefit comes from longer sequences: as sequence length grows, the quadratic attention computation dominates over communication and other overheads, making each training step increasingly compute-efficient. Each step also processes proportionally more tokens, so throughput scales with sequence length. At 64K, SP=4 processes 13,396 tokens/second — 3.7x the baseline.

These results use only 4 GPUs with SP=4. With 8 GPUs (SP=8), you can push to even longer sequences — up to 256K+ tokens — or use 2D parallelism (SP=4, DP=2) to combine long-context training with data-parallel throughput.

Use flash_attention_2 for Ampere GPUs, or flash_attention_3 for Hopper GPUs. Wait for flash_attention_4 on Blackwell 🕰.

#10067. Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon

Edge AI complements the cloud to bring the best AI experiences. These rely on a continuous flow of context and intelligence across both, working as a model cascade where information is captured and processed in the right place at the right time. Ultra-low-power models on the edge can continuously sense and respond in real time, while seamlessly handing off to larger on-device or cloud models when deeper reasoning is needed.

Still, building for the edge is much harder than it should be. While cloud infrastructure has converged around a few standard software stacks, the edge is split across hundreds of proprietary chip architectures and incompatible toolchains. For ML developers, this creates a heavy fragmentation tax, where you end up rewriting kernels, re-quantizing models, and debugging vendor-specific compilers for every chip you target.

Last year, Google Research introduced Coral NPU with a simple idea: an open hardware and software standard is the only way to unify the edge and unlock developer productivity and portability. Our standards based, ML-first RISC-V architecture paired with a reliable open-source toolchain gives developers confidence that their models will compile and run, letting teams optimize a model once and deploy it across different SoC vendors, devices, and power envelopes.

Today, we are reaching three major milestones in the Coral effort:

Fixing fragmentation at the edge takes more than publishing an instruction set. Historically, many edge accelerators were designed to hit high peak-compute numbers on spec sheets, leaving compiler teams to figure out software support later. In practice, unsupported neural network layers fall back to a general-purpose CPU, which can hurt latency and drain the battery.

We designed the Coral NPU architecture and its compiler together from the start. Instead of chasing peak metrics, our focus is on energy-viable compute: helping to deliver the right performance at the right power envelope for your application.

Over the past year, we released the first three milestones of the 32-bit Coral NPU design: a C-programmable RISC-V scalar frontend for control flow (Milestone 1), an RVV v1.0 vector co-processor for SIMD operations (Milestone 2), and a tightly coupled memory subsystem with floating point support (Milestone 3). With this month's release of the Matrix Execution Unit (Milestone 4), the 32-bit architecture is complete.

Scalar and vector units are great for general control logic and signal processing, but modern ML workloads—from vision encoders to transformer attention layers—spend most of their time on 2D matrix-matrix (GEMM) and matrix-vector (GEMV) multiplication. Running 2D matrix math on a 1D vector engine forces the chip to repeatedly load weights and activations from memory, which can mean spending more energy moving data than doing math.

Our Matrix Execution Unit leverages the RISC-V VME specification (formally part of the Zvt family) to address this need and uses a dedicated outer-product multiply-accumulate (MAC) engine. Because an outer-product engine computes a full 2D tile of operations in a single cycle (256 MACs per cycle), it reuses weights and activations directly inside local registers. This brings quadratic throughput scaling to the core, configurable for up to 1 TOPS.

Having a dedicated matrix engine in a sub-10 mW envelope changes what developers can build on a small battery. Rather than stopping at simple keyword spotting or basic motion detection, devices can run continuous, multimodal workloads, including compact transformer models like Gemma, real-time voice translation on wearables, spatial audio filtering on hearables, and low-latency visual perception on robots.

To help silicon teams bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub.

To make the hardware easy to target without writing custom assembly, we are also releasing the v1.0 foundation of our open-source MLIR/IREE compiler toolchain.

With this stack, you can bring models from JAX, PyTorch, or TensorFlow through standard representations like StableHLO and TOSA. The compiler partitions workloads between the host CPU and the Coral NPU core, handles operator fusion, tiles matrices to fit local SRAM and matrix accumulators, and progressively lowers workloads directly to Coral NPU scalar, RVV v1.0 vector, and VME matrix instructions. Alongside our open-source MPACT simulator and reference FPGA design, hardware and software teams can benchmark models and tune silicon configurations before a chip ever goes to fabrication.

Turning an open standard into commercial silicon takes collaboration across the entire semiconductor value chain. To help silicon partners bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub, and we are partnering with VeriSilicon on the design implementation and verification (DV) to ensure turnkey readiness for silicon tape-outs. We are also working with GlobalFoundries on their 12LP+ FinFET process - accelerating core timing by 70%, and reducing standard-cell area by up to 15% across RTL iterations, with ongoing evaluation of 12LP+ ultra low-power libraries for the Matrix Execution Unit.

On the commercial silicon side, our collaboration with Synaptics shows how quickly this open standard translates into real hardware across very different power budgets without splitting the software experience.

At Synaptics Tech Day (October 20, 2026), Synaptics is launching three commercial silicon and hardware products built on Coral NPU technology and supported by the open IREE/MLIR toolchain:

Because both product families build on the same architecture and compiler foundation, ML teams can optimize a model once and deploy it to a milliwatt-class wearable (Coralboard SR) or a 1 TOPS board (Coralboard SL) using the same workflow. Developed in collaboration with hardware and System-on-Module partner Grinn, the Coralboard lineup also gives teams a direct path from devkit prototyping to commercial production hardware.

With our 32-bit architecture and v1.0 compiler stack in place, we are already working on the next phase of the roadmap, including a 64-bit Coral NPU architecture and CHERI support for security.

Whether you are designing a custom edge SoC, working on ML compilers, or deploying models to wearables and robotics, Coral NPU can help give you an open path from model to silicon. Here is where you can get started:

We would like to thank the core contributors and leadership team for this work, particularly Billy Rutledge, Ben Laurie, Derek Chow, Shaked Flur, Alex Van Damme, Bilal Khan, David Gao, Gregory Kielian, Julian Mullings-Black, Khaled Talukder, Lun Dong, Matthew Wilson, Michael Hoang, Murali Vijayaraghavan, Naveen Dodda, Roman Lewkow, Stefan Hall, Tor Jeremiassen, Yenkai Wang, Manya Dasari, Akib Uddin, Divya Pandya, Steve He, Preeti Singh, Anthony Phalen, Hans Rempel, Esmeralda Cardenas, Isha Mishra, Katy Zima, Resham Parikh, Hannah Bayer Rushing, Taylor Montgomery, Kai Yick, Srikanth Muroor, Cindy Liu, Bangfei Pan, Alec Go, Geoff Stirling, Robin Dua, Gaurav Arora, Steve Goldberg, Francesco Visin, Gus Martins, Ian Ballantyne, Kat Black, Ravin Kumar, Tris Warkentin, Avinatan Hassidim, Jay Yagnik, Katherine Chou, Shahram Izadi, and Yossi Matias.

#10066. How Text-to-Image AI Generators Work, and 5 Tools That Deliver Good Results

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Type “a lighthouse on a cliff at dusk, oil painting, warm light” into a text box, wait ten seconds, and a picture that never existed appears. It feels like magic, but it is a well-understood pipeline of language models, neural networks and a great deal of math. Knowing how that pipeline works makes you a better prompter, helps you diagnose bad results, and makes it easier to choose the right tool for a job.

This guide explains how text-to-image generators turn words into pixels, why they fail in predictable ways, and how to write prompts that work with the model instead of against it. It then compares five tools that consistently produce good results, starting with Pollo AI, and finishes with a practical workflow, a troubleshooting table and an FAQ. Plans, credits and model versions change often, so confirm current details on each vendor’s site before you commit to a subscription.

Early image generators were mostly GANs, or generative adversarial networks. A GAN pits two networks against each other: a generator that produces images and a discriminator that tries to spot fakes. GANs could produce sharp faces and textures, but they were hard to train, often collapsed into repeating the same few outputs, and were poor at following free-form text.

A second line of research used autoregressive models, which generate an image piece by piece the way a language model generates words. These handled text prompts better but were slow at high resolution.

The shift came with diffusion models. Researchers showed that a network trained to reverse a gradual noising process could generate images with excellent quality and diversity, and that it was far more stable to train than a GAN. Combine that with text conditioning and a compressed image representation, and you get the systems behind most of today’s tools. Newer models increasingly swap the traditional convolutional network for transformers, but the core idea of iterative denoising is still the foundation.

Under the hood, mainstream generators combine three ideas: a way to understand text, a way to represent images compactly, and a way to generate them gradually. The sections below follow a prompt from keystroke to finished picture.

Neural networks cannot read words, so your prompt is first split into tokens, small chunks of text such as whole words or word fragments. A text encoder then converts those tokens into an embedding, a grid of numbers that captures meaning and context. Many systems use encoders trained jointly on images and their captions, so that the text “a red bicycle” and pictures of red bicycles end up close together in the same mathematical space. Some newer systems add a large language model to understand longer, more detailed instructions.

This is why wording matters. The encoder only sees what you wrote, and it has a limited capacity. A short, specific prompt produces a clear signal. A long, rambling one dilutes each instruction.

Instead of drawing on a blank canvas, the model begins with random static. The pattern of that static is controlled by a seed number. The same prompt with a different seed gives a different image, because it starts from different noise. If a tool lets you fix the seed, you can make results repeatable and change just one variable at a time.

During training, engineers take millions of real images and add noise to them in small steps until only static remains. The network is then trained to predict the noise that was added at each step, which teaches it to reverse the process. At generation time, the model applies that skill to pure noise, removing a little at each step. Because it has learned what real images look like, the “noise” it removes gradually reveals something that looks plausible.

Your text embedding is fed into the network through a mechanism called cross-attention. At each step, parts of the evolving image can “look at” relevant parts of the prompt and adjust accordingly. A region that will become a lighthouse attends to the word “lighthouse”. A region that will become the sky attends to “dusk”.

A setting called classifier-free guidance, often shown as guidance scale or prompt strength, controls how strongly each step is pulled toward the prompt. The model computes one prediction with the prompt and one without it, then exaggerates the difference. A low value gives the model freedom and often more natural, varied results. A high value follows the words more literally but can produce oversaturated, over-sharpened or distorted images.

Running diffusion directly on full-resolution pixels would be very expensive. The idea behind Stable Diffusion, known as latent diffusion, is to compress images into a much smaller latent representation using an autoencoder. Denoising happens in that compact space, and a decoder turns the final latent back into a full image. This is a major reason high-quality generation now runs in seconds on a cloud GPU instead of minutes.

The number of denoising steps and the scheduler, which decides how much noise to remove at each step, shape the speed and look of the result. More steps usually add detail up to a point, then give diminishing returns. Many tools hide these settings, but the trade-off is always the same: fewer steps are faster and cheaper, more steps can look more refined.

Most pipelines finish with an upscaler or refinement pass that sharpens detail and fixes small artifacts. Many tools also offer inpainting, which regenerates only a selected region, outpainting, which extends the canvas, and variations, which restart from a related image.

A generator can only produce what it has learned to represent. Models are trained on very large collections of images paired with captions, and the quality, diversity and licensing of that data affect both the output and the legal picture. Models trained on more photographs tend to produce convincing photorealism. Models tuned on illustration and concept art lean toward painterly looks.

This also explains a few behaviors. Common subjects look great because the model has seen thousands of examples. Rare or very specific subjects, such as an unusual machine part or a niche cultural item, often look generic or wrong. Biases in the data can show up as stereotypes, for example in how “a doctor” or “a CEO” is depicted, so it helps to describe the people and setting you actually want.

Understanding the process explains the familiar failures:

Pollo AI’s text to image AI is a browser-based generator built around a simple loop: write a prompt, pick a style, generate, and download. Its page highlights HD output and a wide range of looks, from photorealistic scenes to cute cartoons, anime, pencil sketches, isometric art, abstract compositions and surreal visuals. Files can be downloaded as WebP, PNG or JPEG, a practical spread for web work: WebP keeps pages light, PNG preserves clean edges and transparency-friendly graphics, and JPEG works almost everywhere.

Pollo is also part of a wider platform that covers AI video, so a still image you like can become the starting point for motion without switching ecosystems. That matters for teams producing social content, because one workflow can cover both the image and the short clip built from it.

Things to check: the page does not list specific model names or credit amounts, so review the current plan details before relying on it for high-volume work. Commercial use requires a paid plan.

Best for: quick, versatile image generation across many styles, especially if you also plan to make video.

Midjourney has built its reputation on strong aesthetics. Images tend to arrive with polished composition, dramatic lighting and a distinctive painterly feel, which is why it is popular for concept art, mood boards, album-style visuals and editorial illustration. It offers style references and personalization, so you can steer results toward a consistent look across a project. It also supports editing and variation tools for refining a chosen image.

The trade-offs are practical. It is a paid service, and its prompts reward experimentation over literal instruction following, so you sometimes get something beautiful that is not exactly what you described.

Best for: artistic, high-impact visuals where mood matters more than exact specification.

Adobe Firefly focuses on professional workflows and commercial confidence. Adobe describes Firefly’s own models as trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public-domain material, and it attaches Content Credentials metadata that records AI involvement. It connects with tools many teams already use, including Photoshop features like generative fill and generative expand, which suits designers who edit as much as they generate.

Firefly also provides controls such as style and composition references. Its results can feel cleaner and more commercial than Midjourney’s, which is an advantage for marketing assets and a limitation if you want a wild artistic look.

Best for: marketing and design teams that need editing tools and clearer licensing.

Ideogram is known for rendering legible text inside images, a task where many generators struggle. That makes it a strong choice for posters, social graphics, logo concepts, packaging mockups and product visuals that need a headline or short phrase to read correctly. It also offers style controls and a community gallery that doubles as a prompt library.

Even so, long paragraphs of on-image text can still go wrong. Keep the copy to a few words, put it in quotation marks in the prompt, and describe the lettering style.

Best for: graphics that combine imagery with short, readable text.

Leonardo AI is built for creators who want more control. It offers multiple models, fine-tuning options, image-to-image guidance and a canvas for editing, with a particular following among game artists and designers who need consistent characters and assets. Features such as reference-based generation help keep a character recognizable across many scenes.

The wide set of options is powerful but means a steeper learning curve than a one-box generator, and credit systems can take time to understand.

Best for: consistent characters, game and concept assets, and users who like tuning settings.

A reliable prompt has five parts. Put the most important part first, because it often carries the most weight.

How do text-to-image generators work? They convert your prompt into a numerical representation, then use a diffusion model to remove noise from a random starting image step by step, guided by that representation, until a matching picture appears.

Which text-to-image tool is best? It depends on the job. Pollo AI suits fast, varied generation, Midjourney suits artistic work, Adobe Firefly suits commercial design, Ideogram suits images with text and Leonardo AI suits tuned, consistent assets.

Why does the same prompt give different results? Each run starts from a different random seed. Fixing the seed, where a tool allows it, makes results more repeatable.

Can I use AI-generated images commercially? Often yes, but the rules differ by tool and plan. Pollo, for example, notes that commercial use requires a paid plan. Always check the current terms.

How do I get readable text in an AI image? Use a tool strong at text, keep the wording to a few words, and add the text in a design editor if accuracy is critical.

What file format should I download? WebP for lightweight web pages, PNG for graphics and sharp edges, JPEG for broad compatibility.

Can I turn a generated image into a video? Many platforms support it. Pollo AI, for example, also covers AI video, so you can move from a still to motion in one place.

Text-to-image generators work by turning language into numbers and using those numbers to guide a model that denoises random static into a picture. Once you understand that, prompts stop being guesswork: you give the model a clear subject, style and lighting, you iterate one change at a time, and you fix small flaws locally. Start with a versatile option such as Pollo AI, then add Midjourney, Firefly, Ideogram or Leonardo when a project needs their particular strengths.
